options.B: Mandatory quarantine of all infected families
options.C: Mass drug administration of praziquantel
options.D: Surgical removal of adult worms from patients

explanation: Instead of waiting for individuals to fall sick, health teams treat whole communities—especially school children—all at once to knock down the disease burden. Brilliant public health strategy!

question: A community health nurse is planning a schistosomiasis prevention program in a rural Nigerian village. Which action will provide the most lasting protection?

options.A: Installing clean, accessible piped water and functional sanitation toilets
options.B: Providing free malaria mosquito nets to every household in the village
options.C: Instructing villagers to boil all river water before using it for cooking
options.D: Giving nutritional supplements to adults to boost their body weight

explanation: Clean tap water and proper toilets mean villagers won't need to step into infected streams or contaminate the water sources. That's how we solve the root cause! You're thinking like a true nurse.

question: Which animal is known as the natural reservoir host for the Ebola virus?

options.A: Pigs on farms
options.B: Domestic dogs
options.C: Fruit bats
options.D: Cattle and goats

explanation: Spot on! Fruit bats carry the virus naturally without getting sick themselves. Think of them as the original home of the virus in nature.

question: Why do we call Ebola a zoonotic disease?

options.A: It spreads exclusively among wild animals in the forest
options.B: It can only be transmitted through contaminated water
options.C: It mutates rapidly inside human respiratory tracts
options.D: It originates in animals and spreads to humans

explanation: You got it! 'Zoonotic' simply means an infection that jumps from animals to humans. Easy peasy!

question: When the Ebola virus enters the human body, which immune cells does it attack first?

options.A: Red blood cells and platelets
options.B: Epithelial cells of the skin
options.C: Macrophages and monocytes
options.D: Neuron cells in the brain

explanation: Spot on! The virus tricks our body by attacking our own defense cells (macrophages and monocytes) right from the start.

question: A community health nurse is teaching villagers how Ebola spreads. Which practice should she warn against the most?

options.A: Drinking boiled water from a community well during dry seasons
options.B: Eating well-cooked pork from certified local livestock farms
options.C: Washing the body of a relative who died from suspected Ebola
options.D: Sharing eating utensils with a family member who has malaria

explanation: Well done! The viral load is super high in someone who just passed away, making traditional burial touching very risky.

question: What is the usual incubation period range for Ebola?

options.A: 2 to 21 days
options.B: 1 to 3 hours
options.C: 6 months to a year
options.D: 30 to 60 days

explanation: Correct! Symptoms can show up anywhere from 2 days to 3 weeks after contact. That's why monitoring takes up to 21 days.

question: Which signs and symptoms usually show up first when a person is coming down with Ebola?

options.A: Sudden fever, fatigue, and severe muscle aches
options.B: Profuse internal bleeding and skin bruising
options.C: Paralysis of the lower limbs and blindness
options.D: Productive cough and severe chest congestion

explanation: You nailed it! Early Ebola can easily feel like malaria or typhoid at first—sudden fever and body weakness are the major clues.

question: Why is it so important to quickly isolate a suspected Ebola patient in a clinic?

options.A: It allows the lab to make local drugs
options.B: It prevents the virus from spreading to other patients and healthcare staff
options.C: It eliminates the need to wear protective gowns
options.D: It cures the patient before bleeding starts

explanation: Spot on! Isolating patients cuts off the transmission chain immediately and keeps everyone else in the ward safe.

question: What is the gold-standard laboratory test used to confirm an Ebola infection?

options.A: Routine microscopic examination of red blood cells
options.B: X-ray imaging of the chest
options.C: Stool microscopy for parasites
options.D: Reverse transcription-polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR)

explanation: Correct! RT-PCR is the reliable test that catches the virus's RNA in blood samples.

question: What is the main focus of nursing care for a patient with Ebola?

options.A: Administering high-dose broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Placing the patient on complete bed rest without food or water
options.C: Providing supportive care like fluid replacement and symptom relief
options.D: Surgically removing infected lymph nodes

explanation: You got it! Since it's a virus, nursing care is all about keeping the patient hydrated and comfortable while their immune system fights.

question: An Ebola patient is vomiting and having terrible watery diarrhea. What is the nurse's priority action?

options.A: Stop all oral meds until diarrhea clears up
options.B: Start aggressive rehydration therapy to correct fluid and electrolyte losses
options.C: Restrict all oral fluids to give the tummy a rest
options.D: Apply warm compresses to stop belly cramps

explanation: Spot on! Replacing lost fluids quickly is lifesaving because dehydration and shock are the big dangers here.

question: Which part of wearing Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) is most risky for accidentally contaminating yourself?

options.A: Donning (putting on) the clean gear
options.B: Storing unused aprons
options.C: Doffing (removing) the contaminated gear
options.D: Walking through the hallway

explanation: Correct! Taking off dirty gear takes the most care because you might accidentally touch germs on the outside. Always follow the steps carefully!

question: Which of these is a BIG NO-ROUTINE in infection control during an Ebola outbreak?

options.A: Decontaminating room surfaces with chlorine solutions
options.B: Reusing disposable gloves after washing them with ordinary soap
options.C: Limiting the number of staff entering the isolation zone
options.D: Using a trained buddy to watch you remove your PPE

explanation: You got it! Disposable gloves are strictly one-time-use. Never wash and reuse them—safety first!

question: How long must close contacts of an Ebola patient be watched for signs of illness?

options.A: 5 days
options.B: 3 months
options.C: 48 hours
options.D: 21 days

explanation: Spot on! Since the incubation period is up to 21 days, we keep track of contacts for that full period to catch any early signs.

question: Why is building trust with the community so vital during an Ebola outbreak?

options.A: It stops the virus from becoming airborne
options.B: It lets the government cancel travel bans
options.C: It prevents families from hiding sick relatives and encourages early reporting
options.D: It gives clinic staff higher pay

explanation: Correct! When people trust health workers, they bring sick family members in early instead of hiding them, which stops the spread.

question: What do we mean by Post-Ebola Syndrome?

options.A: A collection of chronic physical symptoms persisting after recovery
options.B: A permanent mental illness from the incubation period
options.C: An acute respiratory infection before fever starts
options.D: A sudden relapse of active internal bleeding on day two

explanation: You got it! Even after beating the virus, survivors can deal with lingering joint pain, fatigue, and vision issues.

question: What crucial advice must a nurse give to a male patient who has just recovered from Ebola?

options.A: Return to the isolation ward immediately for another vaccine
options.B: Use barrier contraception or practice safe sex because the virus can linger in semen
options.C: Take daily antibiotics to clear the virus from your joints
options.D: Avoid all physical contact with family forever

explanation: Spot on! The virus can hide in certain body fluids long after recovery, so safe sex guidance is a must for male survivors.

question: What is the main virus that causes COVID-19?

options.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.B: SARS-CoV-2
options.C: Influenza A virus
options.D: Respiratory Syncytial Virus

explanation: COVID-19 stands for coronavirus disease 2019, and it is caused by the specific virus called Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome Coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2). You've got this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which part of the COVID-19 virus helps it attach to human cells?

options.A: Lipid capsules
options.B: Peptidoglycan walls
options.C: Flagella tails
options.D: Spike proteins

explanation: Think of the spike proteins as tiny crowns on the outside of the virus that latch onto human cells to start an infection. Great job! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h1)

question: Which human cell receptors does SARS-CoV-2 mainly latch onto?

options.A: Cholinergic receptors
options.B: Insulin receptors
options.C: ACE2 receptors
options.D: Beta-adrenergic receptors

explanation: ACE2 receptors are found in large amounts in our lung tissue, making them the main doorway for the virus to enter the body. Keep it up! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h2)

question: What is the main danger of a cytokine storm in severe COVID-19 patients?

options.A: A sudden drop in core body temperature
options.B: Severe tissue damage from a hyperactive immune response
options.C: Permanent loss of the sense of taste and smell
options.D: Complete shut down of bone marrow white blood cell production

explanation: A cytokine storm happens when the immune system goes into overdrive, flooding the lungs with chemicals that end up harming healthy tissue. You're learning fast! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h2)

question: Which symptom is uniquely linked to COVID-19 compared to many other common respiratory infections?

options.A: Loss of taste or smell
options.B: Yellow skin discoloration
options.C: Uncontrollable muscle spasms
options.D: Severe joint stiffness

explanation: While many bugs give you a cough and fever, suddenly losing your sense of taste or smell is a classic sign of COVID-19. Well spotted! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h3)

question: A patient has a breathing rate of 32 breaths per minute and an oxygen level of 91% on room air. How is this classified?

options.A: Asymptomatic infection
options.B: Mild illness
options.C: Severe illness
options.D: Moderate illness

explanation: An oxygen level below 94% along with fast breathing means the patient is struggling and needs urgent care. You can totally master this! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h3)

question: Why do hospitals immediately isolate patients showing respiratory symptoms?

options.A: To speed up the administration of intravenous fluids
options.B: To reduce the cost of diagnostic testing supplies
options.C: To prevent transmission to staff and other patients
options.D: To allow patients to sleep without hospital noise

explanation: Isolating patients right away stops airborne droplets from spreading to other vulnerable people in the clinic. Smart nursing practice! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h4)

question: What does 'silent hypoxia' mean in COVID-19 patients?

options.A: A complete absence of lung sounds during stethoscope auscultation
options.B: Normal breathing rates paired with severe panic attacks
options.C: Elevated carbon dioxide levels despite normal oxygen saturation
options.D: Dangerously low blood oxygen levels without the feeling of breathlessness

explanation: Some patients have critically low oxygen on monitors yet feel completely fine, which can be tricky and dangerous. Good to know for clinicals! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h4)

question: Why are awake COVID-19 patients sometimes asked to lie on their stomachs (prone positioning)?

options.A: It completely eliminates the need for oxygen therapy
options.B: It makes it easier to insert nasogastric feeding tubes
options.C: It improves lung expansion and oxygen exchange
options.D: It prevents patients from developing pressure ulcers

explanation: Proning helps open up parts of the lungs that usually get squished, helping the patient breathe much better. Every day you're building clinical skills! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h5)

question: What type of medicine is often given to hospitalized COVID-19 patients to prevent blood clots?

options.A: Anticoagulants
options.B: Antipyretics
options.C: Antihistamines
options.D: Antibiotics

explanation: COVID-19 can make the blood more likely to clot, so doctors routinely prescribe blood thinners (anticoagulants) to keep patients safe. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h5)

question: What do we call health issues that linger for weeks or months after recovering from COVID-19?

options.A: Acute rebound syndrome
options.B: Secondary convalescence
options.C: Long COVID
options.D: Delayed viral shedding

explanation: When symptoms stick around long after the initial infection is gone, it's known as Long COVID. You're making steady progress! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which of these is a very common complaint from people dealing with Long COVID?

options.A: Chronic fatigue and brain fog
options.B: Permanent paralysis of the lower limbs
options.C: Uncontrollable weight gain within days
options.D: Total loss of long-term childhood memories

explanation: Many patients struggle with extreme tiredness and trouble focusing long after testing negative. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h6)

question: Which mask must nurses wear during procedures that generate aerosols on COVID-19 patients?

options.A: Plastic face shield alone
options.B: Cloth face covering
options.C: Standard paper surgical mask
options.D: N95 respirator

explanation: Procedures that kick tiny droplets into the air require a tight-fitting N95 mask to keep you safe. Safety first in nursing! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h7)

question: Which of these actions is WRONG when trying to stop the spread of respiratory viruses in a hospital?

options.A: Reusing disposable single-use gloves between multiple patients
options.B: Ensuring proper room ventilation in clinical spaces
options.C: Performing hand hygiene before and after patient contact
options.D: Cleaning high-touch environmental surfaces regularly

explanation: Single-use gloves are meant for one patient only! Reusing them is a sure way to spread germs around. You'd never make that mistake! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h7)

question: What is the main goal of getting widespread COVID-19 vaccinations?

options.A: Prevention of all future bacterial lung infections
options.B: Prevention of severe disease, hospitalization, and death
options.C: Complete eradication of all human coronaviruses worldwide
options.D: Immediate elimination of the need for hand washing

explanation: Vaccines help train your immune system so that even if you catch the virus, you are much less likely to get severely sick or end up in the hospital. Brilliant! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h8)

question: How should a nurse best handle a patient who is hesitant about taking a vaccine?

options.A: Use empathetic communication and provide clear, factual information
options.B: Insist that vaccination is mandatory without discussion
options.C: Ignore their concerns and focus only on willing patients
options.D: Warn them that refusal will result in legal penalties

explanation: Listening patiently and addressing fears with kindness and facts is the best way to build trust. Great nursing communication! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T12#GNS214_U1_T12_h8)

question: What is the primary physiological defect in Type 1 diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.B: Peripheral resistance to the action of insulin
options.C: Temporary glucose intolerance during pregnancy
options.D: Excessive production of glucagon by the liver

explanation: Type 1 diabetes occurs when the immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys the insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h1)

question: Why does hyperglycemia occur in patients with diabetes mellitus?

options.A: Dietary protein is converted directly into simple sugars
options.B: Cells fail to absorb glucose due to insulin problems
options.C: The kidneys actively produce excess glucose from water
options.D: The liver stores too much glycogen and refuses to release it

explanation: Without enough effective insulin, glucose cannot enter body cells for energy and instead stays building up in the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h1)

question: What does the term polyuria mean in a patient with diabetes?

options.A: Severe pain and burning sensation during urination
options.B: Excessive production and passing of urine
options.C: A sudden and total inability to pass any urine
options.D: An intense, constant craving for sweet foods

explanation: Polyuria refers to passing large volumes of urine, which happens when excess sugar pulls extra water out of the body. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h2)

question: A patient comes to the clinic complaining of constant thirst, frequent urination, and sudden weight loss. What condition should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Chronic kidney disease
options.B: Diabetes mellitus
options.C: Urinary tract infection
options.D: Iron deficiency anemia

explanation: The classic trio of excessive thirst, frequent urination, and unexplained weight loss strongly points toward new-onset diabetes mellitus. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h2)

question: What does an HbA1c test measure in a patient with diabetes?

options.A: How well the kidneys are filtering waste products from blood
options.B: The exact amount of insulin currently stored in the liver
options.C: Average blood sugar levels over the past three months
options.D: Immediate blood glucose level at the exact time of the test

explanation: HbA1c measures glucose attached to hemoglobin red blood cells, reflecting average control over their lifespan of about three months. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h3)

question: Why is self-monitoring of blood glucose important for a patient managing diabetes?

options.A: It cures the underlying insulin resistance in Type 2 diabetes
options.B: It helps track daily blood sugar patterns and guide safe care
options.C: It prevents the patient from ever experiencing low blood sugar
options.D: It completely replaces the need for clinic check-ups and lab tests

explanation: Checking blood sugar at home gives immediate feedback on how food, activity, and medicine affect glucose levels day-to-day. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h3)

question: Which medication is typically prescribed as the first-line oral treatment for Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Regular insulin
options.B: NPH insulin
options.C: Metformin
options.D: Glibenclamide

explanation: Metformin is universally recommended as the starting oral drug because it lowers blood sugar effectively without causing weight gain or low blood sugar on its own. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h4)

question: Why must nurses instruct patients on insulin therapy to rotate their injection sites?

options.A: To make sure the injection needle stays sharp for every single dose
options.B: To prevent abnormal fatty lumps or tissue damage under the skin
options.C: To speed up the onset time of long-acting insulin preparations
options.D: To ensure the insulin is absorbed directly into the stomach lining

explanation: Injecting in the exact same spot repeatedly causes lipodystrophy, which ruins skin tissue and alters how evenly insulin is absorbed. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h4)

question: How does regular physical activity benefit a patient with Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: It helps body cells respond better to available insulin
options.B: It allows the patient to eat unlimited amounts of sugar
options.C: It permanently repairs destroyed cells inside the pancreas
options.D: It replaces the daily need for checking blood sugar levels

explanation: Exercise makes muscle and tissue cells more sensitive to insulin, allowing glucose to move out of the blood and into cells more easily. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h5)

question: What dietary advice is most appropriate for a nurse to give a patient managing Type 2 diabetes?

options.A: Eliminate all forms of carbohydrates completely from the diet
options.B: Rely entirely on fruit juices for daily hydration and energy
options.C: Choose high-fiber foods and practice moderate portion control
options.D: Eat only once a day to keep blood sugar levels completely flat

explanation: Balanced nutrition focuses on whole grains, fiber, and sensible portions rather than dangerous elimination diets. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h5)

question: Which of the following is an acute complication of diabetes caused by dangerously low blood sugar?

options.A: Diabetic ketoacidosis
options.B: Diabetic retinopathy
options.C: Peripheral neuropathy
options.D: Hypoglycemia

explanation: Hypoglycemia happens when blood glucose drops too low, triggering symptoms like shaking, sweating, and confusion that require quick treatment. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h6)

question: Why are patients with long-term diabetes at high risk for foot ulcers and amputations?

options.A: Nerve damage and poor blood flow reduce feeling and healing
options.B: Daily physical exercise wears down the bones in the lower legs
options.C: High blood sugar makes the skin on the feet extremely fragile
options.D: Patients naturally lose interest in cleaning and drying their feet

explanation: Neuropathy prevents patients from feeling minor injuries, while poor circulation stops those injuries from healing properly, leading to severe ulcers. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of patient education in diabetes management?

options.A: To ensure the patient memorizes complex medical terminology
options.B: To shift all responsibilities of treatment onto family members
options.C: To empower the patient to safely manage their daily care
options.D: To eliminate the need for any follow-up visits at the clinic

explanation: Since diabetes is a daily home-managed condition, education equips patients with the skills needed to make safe lifestyle and treatment decisions. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h7)

question: How do community support groups help individuals living with diabetes?

options.A: By supplying free prescription medications to every attendee
options.B: By reducing isolation and sharing practical coping strategies
options.C: By diagnosing new medical complications before doctors do
options.D: By replacing professional nursing care with traditional remedies

explanation: Support groups offer emotional encouragement and practical advice from peers who truly understand the daily realities of living with a chronic illness. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T13#GNS214_U1_T13_h7)

question: What does the systolic blood pressure reading measure?

options.A: The pressure when the heart rests
options.B: The total volume of blood in the body
options.C: The pressure when the heart beats
options.D: The speed of blood flow in veins

explanation: Systolic pressure represents the force in the arteries when the heart muscle contracts to pump blood forward. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why don't we diagnose someone with high blood pressure (hypertension) after just one high reading?

options.A: Nigerian guidelines require at least five months of tracking
options.B: Blood pressure machines only work accurately on the third try
options.C: Systolic pressure changes constantly based on what food was eaten
options.D: Temporary factors like stress or rushing can falsely raise readings

explanation: Things like rushing to the clinic, traffic anxiety, or pain can make BP jump temporarily. That's why we always check a few times before making a diagnosis. Great job thinking like a nurse!

question: Primary hypertension is also frequently called what?

options.A: Secondary hypertension
options.B: Gestational hypertension
options.C: Reversible hypertension
options.D: Essential hypertension

explanation: We call it 'essential hypertension' when high blood pressure happens on its own without another clear medical condition causing it. Easy peasy!

question: Which of the following is a modifiable risk factor for hypertension?

options.A: Family genetic history
options.B: Chronological aging
options.C: Biological sex
options.D: High dietary salt intake

explanation: Modifiable risk factors are lifestyle habits or conditions that a person can change, such as reducing salt intake, unlike age or genetics. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h2)

question: Why is hypertension frequently called the 'silent killer'?

options.A: It usually causes no symptoms in its early stages
options.B: Patients refuse to talk about their diagnosis
options.C: It stops the heart without any warning sounds
options.D: It only affects people who are sleeping

explanation: Because high blood pressure rarely causes physical discomfort initially, individuals often remain unaware of their condition until complications arise. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T14#GNS214_U1_T14_h3)

question: If a patient has severe hypertension, which symptom might they complain about?

options.A: Severe pain in the lower abdomen
options.B: Morning occipital headaches
options.C: Sudden swelling in both feet
options.D: Uncontrolled trembling of hands

explanation: A pounding headache right at the back of the head (occipital area) when waking up is a classic warning sign of very high pressure. Keep storing these clinical pearls!

question: What happens to a patient's blood pressure reading if you use a cuff that is too small for their arm?

options.A: The blood pressure reading will be falsely low
options.B: The mercury column will fail to rise at all
options.C: The reading will remain completely normal
options.D: The blood pressure reading will be falsely high

explanation: A tiny cuff squeezes too hard against a big arm, making the reading look much higher than it really is. Always match your cuff size to the patient!

question: How long should a patient sit quietly before you measure their blood pressure?

options.A: No rest time is needed
options.B: At least thirty minutes
options.C: At least five minutes
options.D: Exactly one hour

explanation: Giving them 5 minutes to sit and breathe lets walking, talking, or anxiety settle so you get an accurate baseline reading.

question: What is the main goal of the DASH diet for someone with high blood pressure?

options.A: To increase potassium, calcium, and fiber while reducing sodium
options.B: To replace all fluid intake with specialized herbal teas
options.C: To encourage rapid weight loss through strict calorie counting
options.D: To eliminate all carbohydrates from the daily meal plan

explanation: DASH focuses on whole foods packed with good minerals like potassium and calcium while cutting back on salt to protect the heart.

question: Which of these is NOT a good lifestyle change for managing high blood pressure?

options.A: Engaging in regular aerobic exercise
options.B: Increasing dietary sodium intake
options.C: Stopping tobacco smoking completely
options.D: Limiting heavy alcohol consumption

explanation: More salt (sodium) holds onto water in the body and pushes blood pressure up—definitely something we want patients to cut back on!

question: A patient says, 'My BP is normal today, so I'll stop my drugs.' What is the best way for a nurse to reply?

options.A: Suggest replacing the prescribed drugs with local palm wine
options.B: Agree that normal readings mean the disease has gone away permanently
options.C: Tell the patient to double the dose whenever they feel dizzy
options.D: Explain that the medication controls the condition rather than curing it

explanation: Normal readings just mean the medication is doing its job! Stopping it will cause the pressure to shoot right back up. Patient education is key!

question: What does the term 'orthostatic hypotension' mean?

options.A: A sudden drop in blood pressure when standing up
options.B: Swelling in the lower legs due to poor circulation
options.C: A spike in heart rate after eating heavy meals
options.D: High blood pressure caused by sleeping flat on the back

explanation: When blood vessels are slow to adjust to a new position, standing up too fast can cause a dizzy spell because of a sudden drop in pressure. Good to know for patient safety!

question: What is the main difference between hypertensive urgency and a hypertensive emergency?

options.A: Whether the patient is male or female
options.B: The time of day the blood pressure was checked
options.C: The exact numerical value of the diastolic reading
options.D: The presence of acute target organ damage

explanation: Urgency means extremely high pressure, but emergency means the high pressure is actively harming vital organs like the heart or brain. Big difference in how fast we act!

question: A patient arrives at the clinic with a BP of 220/130 mmHg, chest pain, and confusion. What are they likely experiencing?

options.A: Normal white coat syndrome
options.B: Isolated systolic hypertension
options.C: Hypertensive urgency
options.D: Hypertensive emergency

explanation: Extremely high blood pressure plus signs of brain or heart distress (like confusion and chest pain) makes this a critical medical emergency. You're crushing these clinical scenarios!

question: What is the main thing that makes cancer cells different from normal body cells?

options.A: Growing and spreading without normal body control
options.B: Destroying tissues only when bacteria are present
options.C: Stopping all cell division permanently
options.D: Sudden shrinkage of major organs

explanation: Think of normal cells as following strict traffic rules, while cancer cells throw out the rulebook and multiply uncontrollably. You've got this!

question: Why is it super important for nurses in primary health clinics to know about cancer?

options.A: Primary health centers run all national chemotherapy programs
options.B: Infectious diseases are no longer treated in Nigeria
options.C: Community clinics handle complex surgeries daily
options.D: Nurses are usually the first health workers patients see with early symptoms

explanation: Spotting early signs at the grass-roots level means we can refer patients quickly and save lives. Great nursing starts in the community!

question: What do we call the process when cancer cells break away and travel to other parts of the body?

options.A: Apoptosis
options.B: Hyperplasia
options.C: Metastasis
options.D: Initiation

explanation: Metastasis is just the medical term for cancer packing its bags and traveling through the blood or lymph to start a new tumor elsewhere. You're mastering the terms!

question: What actually happens during the 'promotion' stage of cancer development?

options.A: Mutated cells are stimulated to divide over and over
options.B: Cancer cells immediately travel to the brain
options.C: All abnormal cells safely destroy themselves
options.D: Normal DNA is completely repaired by enzymes

explanation: During promotion, things like lifestyle factors or irritants encourage those already-changed cells to keep multiplying into a bigger problem.

question: Which common virus is strongly linked to the development of cervical cancer?

options.A: Human Immunodeficiency Virus
options.B: Human Papillomavirus
options.C: Epstein-Barr virus
options.D: Hepatitis B virus

explanation: High-risk strains of HPV can cause changes in cervical cells over time. This is why screening and the HPV vaccine are such big wins in public health!

question: A 45-year-old woman comes to the clinic with a hard, painless breast lump she noticed six months ago. What often causes this kind of late presentation in our communities?

options.A: Cultural stigma and trying alternative therapies first
options.B: The lump grew instantly overnight
options.C: Routine mammograms are done everywhere
options.D: The tumor was already surgically removed

explanation: Fear, stigma, and trying traditional remedies first are real barriers our patients face. As nurses, part of our job is compassionate, judgment-free education.

question: Which viral infection is a major risk factor for liver cancer?

options.A: Influenza A
options.B: Hepatitis B
options.C: Varicella Zoster
options.D: Rabies virus

explanation: Chronic Hepatitis B causes long-term inflammation and scarring in the liver, which can eventually lead to liver cancer. Vaccination is key!

question: Why is smoking tobacco such a major risk factor for many types of cancer?

options.A: It introduces living cancer cells into the lungs
options.B: It blocks all major blood vessels
options.C: It contains harmful chemicals that damage cellular DNA
options.D: It stops red blood cells from forming

explanation: Tobacco smoke has active chemical carcinogens that mess up the genetic code inside healthy cells, triggering abnormal growth.

question: During a Visual Inspection with Acetic Acid (VIA) screening for cervical pre-cancer, what liquid is applied to the cervix?

options.A: Iodine tincture
options.B: Vinegar
options.C: Hydrogen peroxide
options.D: Normal saline

explanation: Acetic acid is simply the active ingredient in vinegar! It makes abnormal cells temporarily turn white so the nurse can spot them easily.

question: What is the main purpose of cancer screening programs in primary health care?

options.A: To find out the patient's family tree
options.B: To completely replace laboratory blood tests
options.C: To perform major cancer surgeries
options.D: To catch abnormalities before symptoms and spreading happen

explanation: Screening is all about catching issues early when treatment is easiest and most successful. Prevention is better than cure!

question: In the famous 'CAUTION' warning signs of cancer, what does the letter 'U' stand for?

options.A: Unexplained weight gain
options.B: Urinary tract infection
options.C: Unusual bleeding or discharge
options.D: Ulceration of the skin

explanation: Remember CAUTION! The 'U' reminds us to never ignore unexplained bleeding or discharge from any part of the body. Keep that in your nursing toolkit!

question: A patient has had a hoarse voice and a nagging cough for over three months that won't go away with antibiotics. Which cancer warning sign does this match?

options.A: Difficulty swallowing food
options.B: Obvious change in a mole
options.C: Change in bowel habits
options.D: Nagging cough or hoarseness

explanation: That's the 'N' in CAUTION: a nagging cough or hoarseness. When a symptom sticks around way too long, it's time for a deeper check-up!

question: How should pain medication be given for chronic cancer pain according to standard guidelines?

options.A: Only when the pain becomes unbearable
options.B: Only when the patient remembers to ask
options.C: On a regular schedule around the clock
options.D: Strictly as a single bedtime dose

explanation: Scheduled dosing keeps the pain under control smoothly, rather than waiting for it to spike and trying to chase it down. Smart nursing care!

question: Why do many advanced cancer patients experience severe weight loss and muscle wasting?

options.A: Permanent blockage of the large intestine only
options.B: A total loss of the brain's thirst center
options.C: Being forced to do too much heavy exercise
options.D: Metabolic changes caused by the tumor and treatments

explanation: Cancer changes how the body uses energy, leading to a condition called cachexia where muscle and fat break down fast. Nutritional support is so vital here.

question: What is the primary focus of palliative care?

options.A: To speed up the dying process
options.B: To replace hospital chemotherapy entirely
options.C: To improve quality of life and relieve suffering
options.D: To completely cure aggressive tumors

explanation: Palliative care is all about comfort, dignity, and making sure patients and their families feel supported when a cure isn't possible. Beautiful, compassionate nursing!

question: Why is community health education so crucial for fighting cancer in Nigeria?

options.A: It replaces the need for palliative nurses
options.B: It guarantees free surgeries at every health post
options.C: It helps clear up harmful myths and encourages early hospital visits
options.D: It completely stops genetic mutations from happening

explanation: When we educate our communities with love and facts, we break down fear and cultural barriers so people seek help early. You are going to make a great nurse!

question: What is the primary abnormal protein found in the red blood cells of a person with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Haemoglobin F
options.B: Haemoglobin C
options.C: Haemoglobin A
options.D: Haemoglobin S

explanation: The genetic mutation in sickle cell anaemia specifically leads to the production of abnormal haemoglobin S, which changes the shape of the red blood cells when it loses oxygen. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h1)

question: Why do red blood cells change into a sickle shape in this condition?

options.A: The bone marrow produces cells with too much iron and water inside them
options.B: Haemoglobin S molecules stick together to form rigid rods when they release oxygen
options.C: White blood cells attack and deform the healthy red blood cells
options.D: Excess sugar in the bloodstream causes the red blood cells to shrink and warp

explanation: When haemoglobin S delivers oxygen to body tissues, it clumps into stiff strands that distort the normal round cell into a crescent shape. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h1)

question: What genotype represents a person who carries the sickle cell trait without having the full disease?

options.A: SS
options.B: AA
options.C: SC
options.D: AS

explanation: Genotype AS means the individual has one normal gene and one mutated gene, making them a healthy carrier of the trait. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h2)

question: What must happen for a child to be born with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Only the mother needs to have the full sickle cell disease
options.B: The child must be exposed to severe malaria during infancy
options.C: Both parents must pass on a copy of the mutated sickle cell gene
options.D: Either parent must have genotype AS while the other has genotype AA

explanation: Because it is an autosomal recessive condition, a child needs two copies of the abnormal gene, requiring both parents to contribute a sickle gene. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h2)

question: What is the medical term for the yellowing of the skin and eyes caused by the rapid breakdown of red blood cells?

options.A: Cyanosis
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Pallor
options.D: Erythema

explanation: Jaundice happens when red blood cells break down quickly, releasing excess bilirubin which the liver processes more slowly than it is produced. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h3)

question: Why are children with sickle cell anaemia at a much higher risk of severe bacterial infections?

options.A: Low dietary iron intake weakens the entire immune system from birth
options.B: The bone marrow stops producing white blood cells to make more sickled cells
options.C: Repeated blood vessel blockages eventually damage and destroy spleen function
options.D: Abnormal haemoglobin coats bacteria and prevents immune cells from seeing them

explanation: The spleen filters bacteria and helps fight infections, but repeated sickling clogs its vessels until it stops working entirely, a process called auto-splenectomy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h3)

question: What is the most common trigger for a vaso-occlusive pain crisis in a patient with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Taking daily folic acid supplements
options.B: Dehydration or infection
options.C: Eating high-protein meals
options.D: Sleeping on a firm mattress

explanation: Dehydration thickens the blood and infections increase physical stress, both of which easily trigger blood cells to sickle and block vessels. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h4)

question: A patient with sickle cell anaemia is admitted in a painful vaso-occlusive crisis. Which immediate nursing intervention should be prioritized?

options.A: Preparing the patient for immediate surgical removal of the spleen
options.B: Restricting fluid intake to prevent fluid overload in the lungs
options.C: Administering prescribed pain medication and encouraging fluids
options.D: Encouraging heavy physical exercise to improve circulation

explanation: Managing pain and rehydrating the patient to thin the blood and restore circulation are the immediate priorities during an acute crisis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h4)

question: Which laboratory test is considered the gold standard for confirming a diagnosis of sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Sickle solubility test
options.B: Erythrocyte sedimentation rate
options.C: Haemoglobin electrophoresis
options.D: Full blood count

explanation: Haemoglobin electrophoresis separates the different types of haemoglobin proteins to provide a definitive diagnosis of the specific genotype. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h5)

question: What does an elevated reticulocyte count in a routine blood test usually indicate in a patient with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Iron supplements are building up to toxic levels in the blood
options.B: The patient is experiencing a sudden kidney infection
options.C: The spleen has successfully cleared all abnormal cells from circulation
options.D: The bone marrow is working hard to replace destroyed red blood cells

explanation: Reticulocytes are newly formed red blood cells. A high count shows the bone marrow is rushing to make new cells to make up for those lost to haemolysis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h5)

question: Why is malaria prevention especially critical for individuals living with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Anti-malarial medications cure the underlying genetic mutation permanently
options.B: Malaria infection triggers severe red blood cell sickling and life-threatening crises
options.C: Malaria parasites feed directly on normal adult haemoglobin A exclusively
options.D: Fever from malaria permanently stops the bone marrow from making blood

explanation: Fever, inflammation, and red blood cell destruction caused by malaria are powerful triggers that induce widespread vessel blockage in sickle cell patients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h6)

question: What is the main reason young children with sickle cell anaemia are given daily prophylactic penicillin?

options.A: To prevent severe bacterial infections due to reduced spleen function
options.B: To stop malaria parasites from entering the bloodstream during the rainy season
options.C: To stimulate the bone marrow to produce more flexible red blood cells
options.D: To reduce chronic joint pain caused by dactylitis in the fingers and toes

explanation: Because the spleen loses its ability to filter bacteria early in life, daily penicillin protects these children from dangerous encapsulated bacterial infections. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h6)

question: Which lifestyle advice is most important for a nurse to emphasize during patient education for sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: Restrict fluid intake in the evening to prevent frequent nighttime urination
options.B: Maintain consistent daily hydration and avoid extreme temperature changes
options.C: Wear tight, supportive clothing to keep the peripheral blood vessels compressed
options.D: Engage in intense competitive sports to build strong cardiovascular endurance

explanation: Drinking plenty of water prevents the blood from thickening, and avoiding cold temperatures stops blood vessels from narrowing, both of which prevent crises. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h7)

question: A mother brings her young child with sickle cell anaemia to the clinic. Which statement by the mother shows she understands home care instructions?

options.A: We stopped the daily penicillin because our child has not been sick lately
options.B: We avoid letting our child eat any green vegetables containing folic acid
options.C: I only give pain medication when the swelling in the fingers becomes unbearable
options.D: I make sure my child drinks plenty of water every day, even when feeling well

explanation: Consistent daily hydration keeps red blood cells flowing smoothly and is a cornerstone of preventing painful vaso-occlusive episodes at home. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h7)

question: What is the term for the bone tissue death in the hip or shoulder caused by blocked blood supply in sickle cell patients?

options.A: Avascular necrosis
options.B: Osteomyelitis
options.C: Osteoporosis
options.D: Dactylitis

explanation: Avascular necrosis occurs when restricted blood flow deprives bone tissue of oxygen and nutrients, causing the bone to break down over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h8)

question: Why is regular multi-disciplinary follow-up essential for adults living with sickle cell anaemia?

options.A: To monitor and manage progressive long-term damage to major body organs
options.B: To perform routine blood transfusions that reverse the abnormal gene sequence
options.C: To prevent the patient from ever experiencing another painful crisis again
options.D: To ensure the patient takes daily antibiotics to cure the genetic mutation

explanation: Chronic organ damage to the kidneys, lungs, brain, and joints accumulates over years, requiring coordinated specialist care to catch and treat complications early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T16#GNS214_U1_T16_h8)

question: What is the main goal of good nutrition in Primary Health Care (PHC)?

options.A: Replacing clinical treatments with herbal remedies
options.B: Preventing deficiency diseases and supporting optimal potential
options.C: Eliminating the need for agricultural market regulations
options.D: Reducing the cost of commercial food imports

explanation: You got this! In PHC, good nutrition is all about helping people stay healthy, avoiding illness, and reaching their full body and mind development. Keep it up!

question: Why must community nurses look beyond the clinic when dealing with poor nutrition?

options.A: Because nutrition problems only exist inside large hospital wards
options.B: Because hospital management forbids nurses from talking about food
options.C: Because clinical medications can cure malnutrition completely on their own
options.D: Because root causes like poverty and food disruption require community-based action

explanation: Spot on! Nutritional challenges are often tied to bigger social and economic issues. Giving medicine alone isn't enough—we need community action and education too.

question: What do we call the main nutrients that give the body bulk energy and building blocks?

options.A: Antioxidants
options.B: Electrolytes
options.C: Micronutrients
options.D: Macronutrients

explanation: Great job! Macronutrients include carbs, proteins, and fats. They are the big players that supply your daily energy and physical structure.

question: What does 'hidden hunger' mean in community nutrition?

options.A: Eating enough calories from starchy foods while lacking vital micronutrients
options.B: A sudden shortage of food caused by severe drought conditions
options.C: A psychological condition where patients refuse to eat despite starving
options.D: The physical sensation of hunger felt late at night

explanation: Exactly! Hidden hunger happens when someone gets enough food to fill their stomach (like heavy swallows of starch), but their diet misses the key vitamins and minerals they really need.

question: What is the main use of MUAC tape during community health outreaches?

options.A: To quickly screen for acute malnutrition using a simple tape
options.B: To determine the daily caloric intake of a household
options.C: To test blood sugar levels for diabetes screening
options.D: To calculate the exact body mass index of adult men

explanation: Well done! Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC) uses color-coded tapes to quickly check if infants or young children are suffering from sudden, severe malnutrition.

question: A nurse notices more children losing weight in the months right before the new harvest. What activity helped spot this trend?

options.A: Individual genetic sequencing
options.B: Surgical theater auditing
options.C: Hospital pharmacy inventory check
options.D: Community nutritional status monitoring

explanation: Spot on! Tracking how nutrition changes across different seasons helps nurses spot recurring health issues in the whole community before they get out of hand.

question: What is a big plus of having homestead gardens in rural areas?

options.A: Eliminating the need for any community health education
options.B: Generating large profits on international export markets
options.C: Providing immediate access to fresh vegetables and fruits
options.D: Replacing local health clinics with herbal gardens

explanation: You got it! Homestead gardens mean families can just walk to their backyard to grab fresh, nutritious greens without needing extra cash or long travel.

question: Why is proper post-harvest management important for food security?

options.A: It increases the chemical fertilizer content in staple grains
options.B: It removes the need for farmers to rotate their crops
options.C: It forces farmers to sell all their crops immediately after harvesting
options.D: It prevents food loss from pests and spoilage during lean periods

explanation: Correct! Storing and preserving food properly keeps it safe from pests so families have something to eat even when crops are scarce.

question: What is the main focus of Behavioral Change Communication (BCC) in nutrition?

options.A: Addressing cultural habits and beliefs influencing food choices
options.B: Importing expensive nutritional supplements from abroad
options.C: Enforcing strict legal penalties for poor dietary habits
options.D: Conducting laboratory tests on food chemical safety

explanation: That's right! BCC looks past simple facts to understand the cultural and social reasons behind how people choose and prepare their meals.

question: Why do nurses promote local foods during cooking demos instead of imported ones?

options.A: Local health policies legally forbid the use of foreign recipes
options.B: Local ingredients are usually more affordable and accessible to the community
options.C: Imported foods cause immediate illness in all age groups
options.D: Imported foods are always completely devoid of any nutritional value

explanation: Spot on! Good nutrition teaching has to be practical. Using foods that families can easily buy or grow nearby ensures the habit sticks.

question: Which deficiency condition is marked by severe muscle wasting and very little body fat?

options.A: Night blindness
options.B: Goiter
options.C: Kwashiorkor
options.D: Marasmus

explanation: You're doing great! Marasmus is a severe lack of energy and protein where a child looks extremely thin and wasted away because of absent body fat.

question: What is the primary public health way to prevent iodine deficiency in a population?

options.A: Providing Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Food packets
options.B: Distributing high-dose vitamin A capsules
options.C: Promoting the universal use of iodized salt
options.D: Administering iron-folate tablets to infants

explanation: Correct! Iodized salt is the simplest, most effective way to reach everyone and stop conditions like goiter from developing.

question: What does intersectoral collaboration mean when working on food security?

options.A: Working together across different fields like agriculture, health, and education
options.B: Relying solely on nursing staff to manage agricultural projects
options.C: Merging all hospitals into a single centralized government agency
options.D: Importing food supplies exclusively from neighboring countries

explanation: Spot on! Because food security involves farming, schooling, and healthcare, different ministries and sectors must join hands to fix it.

question: Why is the agricultural sector so important when health workers try to improve nutrition?

options.A: Because farming practices have no impact on community health outcomes
options.B: Because farmers are legally required to diagnose nutritional deficiencies
options.C: Because agricultural workers manage all rural health clinics
options.D: Because agriculture determines how much and what types of food are produced

explanation: Brilliant! Farming dictates what food is available and how varied the food supply is, making agriculture the very foundation of good nutrition.

question: Why do governments create food and nutrition policies?

options.A: To completely ban bringing any foreign food into the country
options.B: To control the exact daily price of goods in local markets
options.C: To manage employment records for all farm workers
options.D: To connect what farmers grow directly with what communities need to stay healthy

explanation: Food policies help make sure that farming output meets the actual nutritional health needs of the population. Great job thinking about the big picture!

question: As a nurse, why is it helpful to understand national food policies?

options.A: Clinical nutritional counseling fails if patients cannot access or afford recommended foods
options.B: Nurses decide the specific types of seeds farmers must plant
options.C: Nurses are legally required to inspect commercial farms for safety
options.D: Clinical staff must directly distribute farming money to local villages

explanation: When you give dietary advice to a patient, you have to know what food is actually available and affordable in their community!

question: What does 'food security' mean for a population?

options.A: Storing a ten-year supply of grains in underground bunkers
options.B: Having military protection around every food warehouse
options.C: Constant physical, social, and economic access to safe and enough food
options.D: Producing every single food item inside the country's borders

explanation: Food security simply means everyone has reliable access to enough safe, nutritious food to live a healthy life.

question: How do government irrigation projects help boost farming?

options.A: By reducing total dependence on seasonal rainfall for farming
options.B: By lowering the market price of chemical fertilizers
options.C: By giving formal land certificates to rural farmers
options.D: By providing cash loans to farmer groups

explanation: Irrigation gives crops water even during dry seasons, which means farmers can grow food all year round.

question: What is the main job of cold chain logistics in the food supply chain?

options.A: To keep transport vehicles cool for drivers on long trips
options.B: To freeze-dry grains for underground storage
options.C: To prevent the rapid spoilage of perishable items like milk and meat
options.D: To kill weed seeds in harvested crops before milling

explanation: Cold chain systems use refrigeration to keep perishable foods fresh and safe all the way from the farm to your plate.

question: Why do bad rural feeder roads hurt national food security?

options.A: They force the government to import all staple foods
options.B: They delay transport, causing high spoilage rates and high food prices in cities
options.C: They stop farmers from getting chemical fertilizers and seeds
options.D: They make it illegal for farmers to sell crops across state lines

explanation: When roads are poor, food gets stuck or damaged on the way, leading to waste and higher prices for people in the city.

question: What is a major cause of post-harvest food loss in farming communities?

options.A: Pest infestations and poor drying techniques
options.B: Strict international export inspections
options.C: Excessive government taxes on farm tools
options.D: Mandatory crop rotation laws from local councils

explanation: Bad storage, pests, and moisture can destroy a huge portion of crops right after harvest before they ever make it to market.

question: Why is making sure grains are properly dried before storage a vital health measure?

options.A: It prevents the growth of molds that produce dangerous aflatoxins
options.B: It stops insects from eating metal storage silos
options.C: It guarantees the seeds will sprout next season
options.D: It makes the grain weigh less during transport

explanation: Wet grain grows mold easily, and that mold makes toxins called aflatoxins that can seriously harm the liver when eaten.

question: Which of these is NOT something food safety regulations normally check for?

options.A: Physical objects like metal shards or stones
options.B: Dangerous levels of chemical pesticide residues
options.C: Political views of the food manufacturing company owners
options.D: Harmful germs causing foodborne illnesses

explanation: Food safety is strictly about biological, chemical, and physical hazards—not who owns the company or what they believe!

question: Why do food safety officers frequently inspect local open-air markets and street food vendors?

options.A: These vendors feed a huge portion of the urban working-class population
options.B: Street vendors have more money to pay official fines
options.C: Open markets never have contamination problems
options.D: Large supermarkets are legally exempt from all safety checks

explanation: Since millions of people buy from local markets and street vendors every day, keeping those foods safe is crucial for public health.

question: What is a key everyday duty for health workers when it comes to food policy?

options.A: Writing the national budget for farm machinery
options.B: Designing state highways for food transport trucks
options.C: Conducting infant growth monitoring to spot early signs of malnutrition
options.D: Issuing business licenses to big food factories

explanation: As health workers, we put policy into action right at the clinic by checking children's growth and catching malnutrition early.

question: A community nurse notices a sudden outbreak of severe diarrhea in one neighborhood. What is the best immediate step?

options.A: Tell all residents to stop eating food completely for a week
options.B: Report the outbreak to local authorities and investigate contaminated food sources
options.C: Request farming grants for local grain producers
options.D: Order heavy machinery to dig up the local market

explanation: Frontline health workers must quickly report suspected outbreaks and trace the source to stop others from getting sick.

question: What is a major challenge that stops agricultural and food policies from succeeding?

options.A: Having too many trained nurses working as policy makers
options.B: Inadequate funding and a lack of follow-through when governments change
options.C: People refusing to eat locally grown foods
options.D: Having too much cold storage in every single village

explanation: Frequent political shifts and poor funding often leave great agricultural policies unfinished.

question: Why do health, agriculture, and environment ministries need to work together on food policies?

options.A: It ensures the health ministry controls the whole budget
options.B: It is just a rule required by international banks
options.C: Food production, safety, and nutrition cut across all of these sectors
options.D: It stops farm workers from practicing nursing in clinics

explanation: Solving big food challenges takes teamwork between farming experts, environmentalists, and healthcare professionals!

question: What is the main goal of doing a nutritional check on a patient in primary health care?

options.A: To evaluate nutritional status and spot early signs of health issues
options.B: To calculate the exact household income of a patient
options.C: To prescribe expensive vitamin supplements for every patient
options.D: To diagnose rare genetic disorders affecting body weight

explanation: Spotting poor nutrition early helps you step in with advice before the patient gets seriously ill. You've got this!

question: Why is it helpful for a nurse to assess the nutrition of an entire family rather than just one person?

options.A: Family members always have identical nutritional requirements
options.B: Individual assessments are legally prohibited in community clinics
options.C: Hospital policies require whole-family admission for dietary advice
options.D: Families usually share similar eating habits and money challenges

explanation: Looking at the whole family helps you see the big picture—like what kind of food is cooked at home and what challenges everyone faces together.

question: Which body measurement is most commonly used in the community to quickly screen young children for severe malnutrition?

options.A: Mid-Upper Arm Circumference (MUAC)
options.B: Total body surface area
options.C: Waist-to-hip ratio
options.D: Head circumference

explanation: The MUAC tape is a nurse's best friend during community outreaches—it's fast, easy, and great for checking young children on the spot!

question: A community nurse needs a quick, easy way to check for sudden fluid loss or weight gain in an adult. What should they use?

options.A: A weighing scale
options.B: A blood pressure cuff
options.C: A skinfold caliper
options.D: A sterile measuring tape

explanation: Never underestimate the power of a simple scale! Regular weighing is the easiest way to catch sudden fluid shifts or weight changes.

question: Which parts of the body usually show signs of vitamin or nutrient shortages first?

options.A: Parts with fast-growing cells like skin, hair, and nails
options.B: Major blood vessels and heart valves
options.C: Hard tissues like bones and deep skeletal muscles
options.D: Internal organs like the liver and kidneys

explanation: Because skin, hair, and nails replace their cells so quickly, they show signs of trouble way before deeper tissues do.

question: Why shouldn't a nurse rely only on visual physical checks when diagnosing malnutrition?

options.A: Clinical signs only appear after the patient is completely cured
options.B: Laboratory tests are illegal to perform in primary health clinics
options.C: Different nutrient shortages can cause very similar physical signs
options.D: Patients usually hide their physical symptoms from healthcare workers

explanation: Many deficiencies look alike on the outside. That's why we always back up our physical exams with diet histories and lab tests!

question: What does 'family food security' mean?

options.A: Having a locked storage room to protect food from insects
options.B: Having reliable access to enough safe, healthy food for everyone
options.C: Eating meals at the exact same time every single day
options.D: Growing all the family food on a private farm without buying anything

explanation: Food security simply means the household consistently has enough safe and nutritious food to live a healthy, active life.

question: What is the main drawback of using a 24-hour food recall to check what a patient eats?

options.A: It requires expensive laboratory equipment to calculate
options.B: Patients may forget or misreport what they actually ate
options.C: It only measures physical height rather than food
options.D: It takes over a week to complete a single interview

explanation: Memory can be tricky! Clients might easily forget that little afternoon snack or misjudge the size of their food portions.

question: Which common lab test is used to screen patients for anemia?

options.A: Liver function enzymes
options.B: Serum lipid profile
options.C: Fast blood glucose
options.D: Hemoglobin and hematocrit

explanation: Checking hemoglobin and hematocrit tells us how well the blood carries oxygen, making it the go-to test for anemia.

question: Why can a sudden infection mess up the results of a patient's blood protein test?

options.A: Infections trigger body changes that alter protein levels regardless of diet
options.B: Lab technicians are not allowed to run protein tests during an illness
options.C: Infections destroy all blood drawing needles in the clinic
options.D: Infection automatically cures any existing vitamin deficiency

explanation: Inflammation from an infection can drive blood protein levels down, which might trick you into thinking the patient is starving when they actually have an infection.

question: Why are infants and young children considered a nutritionally vulnerable group?

options.A: Their rapid growth and development require lots of nutrients
options.B: Their bodies do not require protein during early childhood
options.C: They possess fully developed immune systems that reject food
options.D: They refuse to eat any form of solid food until age five

explanation: Kids grow so fast! If their diet falls short even a little bit, it can quickly lead to poor growth or malnutrition.

question: An elderly patient reports poor appetite, trouble chewing, and losing weight without trying. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: A sudden increase in daily physical growth velocity
options.B: An allergic reaction to drinking clean tap water
options.C: An excessive desire to run marathon races every week
options.D: Age-related dental challenges and a reduced appetite

explanation: As people get older, dental issues, changes in taste, and lower appetite often make eating tougher, putting them at risk of poor nutrition.

question: What should be a nurse's main focus when giving diet advice to a low-income family?

options.A: Advising them to eat only once every two days
options.B: Recommending affordable, locally available foods
options.C: Telling them to stop eating traditional family meals
options.D: Insisting they purchase expensive imported vitamins

explanation: Good nutrition advice has to be practical. Always recommend foods that the family can easily find and afford in their local market.

question: Why should community nutrition counseling respect local food traditions?

options.A: Families are much more likely to follow advice that fits their culture
options.B: Traditional recipes always contain zero nutritional value
options.C: Cultural habits prevent any form of weight gain
options.D: Nurses are legally forbidden from discussing local foods

explanation: When you work with a family's cultural food habits instead of fighting them, they are way more likely to stick with your healthy changes!

question: What does the acronym IEC stand for in public health?

options.A: Immunization, Environment, and Community
options.B: Information, Education, and Communication
options.C: Infection Eradication and Control
options.D: Illness Evaluation and Clinical care

explanation: IEC stands for Information, Education, and Communication, which are the foundational pillars of public health messaging and community health promotion. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T2#GNS214_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why is communication in IEC a two-way process rather than a one-way lecture?

options.A: It is required by government policy for every primary health center.
options.B: It ensures that nurses do not have to speak during health outreaches.
options.C: It allows healthcare providers to listen to community fears and local beliefs.
options.D: It stops patients from asking difficult questions about medications.

explanation: Great nursing is all about listening, not just talking! Two-way communication helps us understand what people are really going through so we can help better.

question: Why do a community diagnosis before starting an IEC campaign?

options.A: Identify the actual health burdens affecting the local population
options.B: Prove that the community lacks basic hygiene practices
options.C: Fulfill administrative paperwork requirements for the local government
options.D: Determine how many nurses are needed for night duty shifts

explanation: You got it! Just like assessing an individual patient before treatment, a community diagnosis helps you find out what health issues are truly troubling the people.

question: A nurse checks clinic attendance registers to see which illnesses bring patients in most often. What is this called?

options.A: Reviewing epidemiological data
options.B: Performing environmental observation
options.C: Conducting cultural mapping
options.D: Establishing peer pressure groups

explanation: Spot on! Looking at clinic records to track disease patterns is a classic way we gather epidemiological data to plan our next steps.

question: What is the main goal of Behavior Change Communication (BCC)?

options.A: Replacing traditional healers with modern doctors
options.B: Ensuring every household buys expensive water filters
options.C: Helping people adopt and sustain healthy lifestyle practices
options.D: Increasing the number of patients admitted to hospital wards

explanation: Exactly! BCC goes beyond just sharing facts; it's about helping people make real, lasting changes that keep them healthy.

question: Why might someone know a health practice is dangerous yet continue doing it?

options.A: They enjoy being sick and visiting the primary health clinic
options.B: Nurses failed to write down the instructions on a chalkboard
options.C: Government laws forbid them from changing their personal habits
options.D: Economic, social, or cultural barriers make the healthy choice difficult

explanation: So true! Knowing what to do is only half the battle. Money, culture, and daily struggles often make healthy choices tough to practice.

question: Which IEC channel works best for reaching a scattered rural population quickly?

options.A: One-on-one clinic counseling
options.B: Detailed written pamphlets
options.C: Radio broadcasts
options.D: Individual home visits

explanation: Correct! Radio is a powerful tool because it travels far and wide, reaching people in remote areas in no time.

question: What is a major downside of relying only on text-heavy pamphlets in a rural community?

options.A: They take too long to read during a surgical procedure.
options.B: They are too expensive for the federal government to print.
options.C: They are ineffective for community members with low literacy levels.
options.D: They encourage people to ignore traditional folk songs.

explanation: Spot on! If people cannot read easily, text-heavy flyers won't help. That's why pictures, radio, and drama are often much better choices.

question: Who should you talk to first when introducing a new health program to a traditional community?

options.A: Newly graduated nursing students from the city
options.B: Commercial transport drivers in the motor park
options.C: International donor agencies and foreign embassies
options.D: Community leaders and traditional rulers

explanation: You got it! Respecting elders and local leaders opens the door for the community to trust and accept your health program.

question: Why is community ownership so important for the long-term success of health projects?

options.A: It guarantees that the clinic will make a profit from drug sales.
options.B: It removes all responsibilities from the shoulders of community nurses.
options.C: Locals will sustain and protect the program after external support ends.
options.D: Government health budgets will no longer be needed at all.

explanation: Exactly! When the community feels the project is theirs, they will keep it running strong long after outsiders pack up and leave.

question: What is the main difference between monitoring and evaluation in a project?

options.A: Monitoring happens after the project ends, while evaluation happens before it starts.
options.B: Monitoring deals with money, while evaluation deals strictly with medicines.
options.C: Monitoring is done by the community, while evaluation is done by politicians.
options.D: Monitoring tracks activities during implementation, while evaluation measures final impact.

explanation: Spot on! Monitoring is what you do while the work is going on, while evaluation checks the final results after everything is done.

question: A nurse wants to make sure new health posters are clear before printing thousands of copies. What should she do?

options.A: Ask doctors in the capital city to review the picture quality
options.B: Distribute all the posters immediately to save transport costs
options.C: Pre-test the posters with a small group of local community members
options.D: Translate the medical text into Latin for a more professional look

explanation: Brilliant! Always pre-test your materials with the target audience first to catch confusing pictures or messages before mass printing.

question: What is the primary goal of nutrition counselling in primary health care?

options.A: Guiding food choices to promote health and prevent disease
options.B: Prescribing expensive nutritional supplements for every patient
options.C: Enforcing strict hospital dietary restrictions on communities
options.D: Diagnosing rare metabolic disorders in a laboratory setting

explanation: Nutrition counselling focuses on helping clients make healthy food choices to prevent illness and support overall wellness in primary care. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why is effective nutrition counselling more than just handing a patient a printed diet sheet?

options.A: It requires understanding the patient's daily life and financial limits.
options.B: Patients in rural communities usually cannot read printed materials.
options.C: Doctors are the only ones legally allowed to explain diet sheets.
options.D: Printed sheets are too expensive to produce in local clinics.

explanation: Real dietary guidance must fit a patient's actual living conditions, budget, and access to local food markets rather than being a generic list. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h1)

question: What physical measurement is commonly used in community settings to quickly screen young children for acute malnutrition?

options.A: Total body water volume
options.B: Resting metabolic rate
options.C: Mid-upper arm circumference
options.D: Sitting height ratio

explanation: Mid-upper arm circumference (MUAC) is a quick, reliable screening tool used by nurses in the field to check for wasting in children. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h2)

question: A nurse wants to know a patient's actual food intake over the past day. Which assessment method is best suited for this?

options.A: A 24-hour dietary recall
options.B: An inpatient surgical biopsy
options.C: A two-week physical exercise log
options.D: A complete genetic blood screening

explanation: The 24-hour dietary recall asks the patient to list all foods and drinks consumed during the previous day to estimate nutrient intake. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h2)

question: Which group is most at risk for protein-energy malnutrition during the transition to family foods?

options.A: Healthy young adult athletes
options.B: Middle-aged male farmers
options.C: Infants and young children
options.D: Retired elderly office workers

explanation: Young children transitioning from breast milk or formula to family foods are at high risk if their new diet lacks sufficient nutrients. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h3)

question: Why do pregnant women have a significantly higher nutritional requirement for specific minerals like iron?

options.A: To support expanding blood volume and fetal growth
options.B: To completely prevent gestational diabetes mellitus
options.C: To replace electrolytes lost through morning sickness
options.D: To cure pre-existing chronic bone infections

explanation: Pregnancy causes a major increase in blood volume and requires extra nutrients to support the developing fetus and placenta. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h3)

question: What communication style works best to encourage a patient to adopt healthier eating habits?

options.A: A silent demonstration with no words
options.B: A strict and formal medical lecture
options.C: A rapid list of commands to follow
options.D: A collaborative and supportive dialogue

explanation: Working together through supportive conversation helps patients feel empowered rather than judged or forced. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h4)

question: Why are open-ended questions preferred over closed questions when taking a dietary history?

options.A: They encourage the patient to share more details about their actual habits.
options.B: They allow the nurse to finish the consultation without speaking.
options.C: They take much less time to complete during busy clinic shifts.
options.D: They legally protect the hospital from documentation errors.

explanation: Open-ended questions prevent patients from giving simple yes or no answers, revealing more accurate information about their true diet. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h4)

question: How should a nurse handle a cultural food taboo that limits a pregnant woman's protein intake?

options.A: Ignore the food taboo completely and focus only on vitamin supplements
options.B: Provide respectful education while suggesting nutritious local alternatives
options.C: Mock the cultural belief to force the patient into immediate compliance
options.D: Report the family to local community authorities for traditional practices

explanation: Respectful dialogue and culturally sensitive education work best to address harmful myths without alienating the patient or community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h5)

question: A mother on a tight budget needs affordable protein sources for her growing toddlers. Which local foods should the nurse recommend?

options.A: Beans, groundnuts, and local fish
options.B: Processed energy bars from abroad
options.C: Expensive dietary protein powders
options.D: Imported canned salmon and caviar

explanation: Locally available plant and animal proteins like beans, groundnuts, and fish are cost-effective and culturally appropriate options. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of scheduling follow-up nutrition appointments with a patient?

options.A: To test the patient's memory on dietary terminology
options.B: To monitor progress and adjust meal plans as needed
options.C: To collect extra administrative fees for the clinic
options.D: To penalize the patient for failing to gain weight

explanation: Follow-ups give nurses a chance to see what is working, troubleshoot new barriers, and keep the patient motivated. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h6)

question: Why is it important for a nurse to identify financial or social barriers before giving a diet plan?

options.A: To comply with federal tax reporting laws for healthcare workers
options.B: To decide whether the patient qualifies for free inpatient medical care
options.C: To prove that the nurse understands the local economic situation
options.D: To ensure the recommended meal plan is realistic and affordable for the family

explanation: Understanding financial limits prevents the nurse from prescribing foods the patient cannot afford or store, ensuring better compliance. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T20#GNS214_U1_T20_h6)
