question: What is the main goal of food safety in primary health care?

options.A: Disease prevention and health promotion
options.B: Regulating international food trade
options.C: Managing surgical theatre sterility
options.D: Treating advanced chronic illnesses

explanation: You've got this! Food safety at the primary health care level is all about stopping foodborne illnesses before they start and helping our communities stay healthy and strong.

question: Why is food safety such a big priority for community health nurses?

options.A: It directly reduces preventable gastrointestinal infections
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for community health clinics
options.C: It is the only way to treat chronic medical conditions
options.D: It stops all forms of malnutrition instantly

explanation: Spot on! When we teach and practice good food safety, we cut down massively on those painful, preventable stomach infections that bring patients into our clinics.

question: Why do we always keep raw meat separate from ready-to-eat foods?

options.A: To speed up the cooking process
options.B: To improve the overall taste of the meal
options.C: To reduce the financial cost of cooking
options.D: To prevent cross-contamination of harmful bacteria

explanation: Think of it like keeping bad company away from good! Separating raw meat stops dangerous germs from jumping onto foods that won't be cooked again before eating.

question: How does putting perishable food in the fridge right away help protect health?

options.A: It turns raw ingredients into ready-to-eat meals
options.B: It completely kills all existing viruses in meat
options.C: It slows down bacterial multiplication in perishable foods
options.D: It removes chemical toxins from spoiled vegetables

explanation: Brilliant! Fridges don't kill bacteria, but the cold temperature acts like a brake, slowing down how fast those tiny germs can grow and multiply.

question: Which specific bacterium causes cholera?

options.A: Staphylococcus aureus
options.B: Salmonella typhi
options.C: Vibrio cholerae
options.D: Escherichia coli

explanation: Great recall! Cholera is caused by *Vibrio cholerae*, a bacterium that loves to hitch a ride in contaminated water and food supplies.

question: A patient comes to your clinic with severe watery diarrhea and sudden, rapid dehydration after eating food from a roadside vendor. What condition should you suspect first?

options.A: Cholera
options.B: Asthma exacerbation
options.C: Chronic hypertension
options.D: Iron deficiency anemia

explanation: You nailed it. Sudden, severe watery diarrhea and rapid dehydration after eating questionable food are classic red flags for cholera. Quick fluid replacement is key here!

question: When washing hands as a food handler, how long should you scrub with soap and water?

options.A: At least twenty seconds
options.B: Until they feel completely dry
options.C: Exactly five seconds
options.D: About two minutes

explanation: Good hygiene is our best shield! Scrubbing with soap for at least twenty seconds gives the soap enough time to lift away and destroy harmful germs.

question: Why is it unsafe to leave frozen meat sitting on a warm kitchen counter to thaw?

options.A: It causes the meat to lose all of its nutritional value
options.B: It freezes the center of the meat even harder
options.C: Surface bacteria multiply rapidly as the outer layers warm up
options.D: It turns the meat into a poisonous chemical substance

explanation: Makes total sense, right? As the outer layers warm up to room temperature, they enter the 'danger zone' where bacteria throw a party and multiply fast.

question: Which of these is NOT a safe way to treat drinking water?

options.A: Adding appropriate chlorine treatment
options.B: Boiling it thoroughly
options.C: Storing it uncovered in a warm, dusty corner
options.D: Using a certified water filtration system

explanation: Exactly! Leaving clean water uncovered is an open invitation for dust, flies, and germs to sneak right back in and contaminate it.

question: How do open refuse dumps contribute to foodborne illnesses in a community?

options.A: They cause the air temperature in the kitchen to rise too high
options.B: They attract pests like flies and rodents that transfer pathogens to food
options.C: They increase the mineral content of nearby groundwater supplies
options.D: They remove all helpful bacteria from the local environment

explanation: You got it! Pests love open garbage; flies and rats feed on the dirt and then march right over uncovers food, leaving dangerous germs behind.

question: Why is it smart for community health nurses to work with local market leaders when promoting food hygiene?

options.A: It stops people from selling food altogether
options.B: It guarantees that the local market will receive government funding
options.C: It helps ensure the hygiene messages are accepted and practiced by vendors
options.D: It allows the nurse to avoid visiting the market stalls personally

explanation: Teamwork makes the dream work! Market leaders are respected, so getting them on board makes food vendors much more willing to listen and adopt safe habits.

question: You notice local food vendors leaving cooked rice uncovered in an open market stall. What is the best first step to take?

options.A: Provide practical education on food protection and cover methods
options.B: Close down all food businesses in the region permanently
options.C: Imprison the vendors without warning or explanation
options.D: Ignore the practice since it is a traditional custom

explanation: Fantastic nursing judgment! As public health nurses, our first superpower is education. Always teach and guide before jumping to harsh punishments.

question: What is the main goal of diet therapy in patient care?

options.A: Modifying regular food intake to meet specific health needs
options.B: Reducing hospital kitchen operational costs
options.C: Ensuring every patient eats the exact same meal
options.D: Replacing all forms of medical drug treatment

explanation: You've got this! Diet therapy is simply tailoring a patient's nutrition to help them heal, manage an illness, or balance their body's needs.

question: Why is diet therapy such an important part of your daily nursing duties?

options.A: Nurses must personally cook all meals served in the hospital ward
options.B: Nurses are responsible for monitoring patient tolerance and supporting the prescribed nutrition plan
options.C: Dietary plans replace the need for physical assessments
options.D: Doctors never check what patients are eating

explanation: Since you spend the most time with patients, you are in the best position to see if they are enjoying their food and how well their body is handling it!

question: When you measure a patient's mid-upper arm circumference and body mass index, what kind of assessment are you doing?

options.A: Environmental factors
options.B: Biochemical data
options.C: Clinical signs
options.D: Anthropometric measurements

explanation: Don't let the big word scare you! 'Anthropometric' just means measuring physical body sizes like height, weight, and arm circumference to check nutrition.

question: You check a patient's lab results, like serum albumin and electrolytes. What type of nutritional data is this?

options.A: Environmental data
options.B: Anthropometric data
options.C: Dietary history
options.D: Biochemical data

explanation: Spot on! Lab tests and blood markers give you biochemical data, showing what is happening inside the patient's body chemically.

question: A patient just had jaw surgery and cannot chew solid foods. Which diet type is best for them?

options.A: High sodium diet
options.B: Standard regular diet
options.C: High residue diet
options.D: Soft or mechanical diet

explanation: Easy choice! Soft and mechanical diets change the texture of food so it's super easy to chew and swallow when the mouth or jaw needs a break.

question: What is a major risk if a recovering patient stays on a clear liquid diet for too long?

options.A: It triggers sudden weight gain from excess fats
options.B: It causes severe high blood pressure
options.C: It permanently ruins the patient's sense of taste
options.D: It can lead to hospital-derived malnutrition due to very low calorie and nutrient content

explanation: Clear liquids are great at first, but they don't have enough energy and nutrients. Keeping patients on them too long starves their healing body!

question: What is the main dietary focus when caring for a patient with high blood pressure (hypertension)?

options.A: Sodium restriction
options.B: Zero fluid consumption
options.C: High protein loading
options.D: Unlimited sugar intake

explanation: You know this! Cutting down on salt (sodium) helps reduce fluid retention and lowers pressure inside the blood vessels.

question: A patient with type 2 diabetes asks why they need to eat more fiber. How should you explain it?

options.A: Fiber slows down digestion, which helps prevent sharp blood sugar spikes after meals
options.B: Fiber increases blood sugar levels rapidly for quick energy
options.C: Fiber completely cures diabetes within a few days of eating it
options.D: Fiber replaces the need to ever take diabetes medication again

explanation: Great nursing communication! Fiber slows down how fast sugar enters the blood, keeping those glucose levels nice and steady after eating.

question: In community health nursing, what are Ready-to-Use Therapeutic Foods (RUTF) mainly used for?

options.A: Replacing clean drinking water supplies
options.B: Treating high blood pressure in adults
options.C: Treating severe acute malnutrition safely at home
options.D: Preserving fresh vegetables without refrigeration

explanation: RUTFs are nutrient-packed pastes that save lives by helping severely malnourished children recover right at home without needing a hospital bed.

question: Why do primary health care nurses encourage families to use local foods like beans and groundnuts for children?

options.A: They contain zero calories and prevent childhood obesity
options.B: They provide affordable, accessible plant proteins and nutrients for growing children
options.C: They completely cure infectious diseases like malaria
options.D: They are the only foods that do not require cooking

explanation: Using cheap, locally available foods makes good nutrition practical and sustainable for everyday families in our communities.

question: Why is it so helpful to involve family members when giving diet counseling to a patient?

options.A: It prevents the patient from ever eating outside the home
options.B: Family members pay all the hospital medical bills
options.C: Family members usually prepare the household meals and manage food purchases
options.D: Family members are legally required to taste all hospital food first

explanation: Since family members are usually the ones cooking at home, bringing them into the conversation ensures the new diet is actually doable for the household!

question: A patient complains that their prescribed diet cuts out all their favorite cultural dishes and feels impossible. What is your best response?

options.A: Tell the patient they have no choice and must strictly obey the prescription
options.B: Work with the patient to find healthy substitutes and modify their favorite cultural meals
options.C: Ignore the complaint since food preferences do not affect health outcomes
options.D: Advise the patient to stop eating entirely until they adjust to the new menu

explanation: That's patient-centered care! Respecting their culture and tweaking their favorite meals makes it much more likely they will stick to the plan.

question: How can you tell over time if a patient's diet therapy is working successfully?

options.A: Weight trends and laboratory values
options.B: The brand of cutlery used for meals
options.C: The exact time the hospital kitchen opens
options.D: The color of the hospital room walls

explanation: Checking changes in body weight and lab results gives you clear, undeniable proof of how well the therapeutic diet is working.

question: What should you suspect first if a patient's lab results don't improve even though they claim to follow their diet?

options.A: The dietary plan, adherence, or overall treatment approach needs re-evaluation
options.B: The patient must be hiding food inside their mattress
options.C: The patient has been cured of the disease completely
options.D: Laboratory tests are never accurate in clinical practice

explanation: When numbers don't budge, it's a cue for the healthcare team to pause, check if the diet is truly working, and make adjustments together.

question: Which insect spreads the malaria parasite to humans?

options.A: Housefly
options.B: Female Anopheles mosquito
options.C: Tsetse fly
options.D: Male Culex mosquito

explanation: Spot on! Malaria is transmitted specifically when an infected female Anopheles mosquito bites looking for a blood meal.

question: Why do pregnant women and young children get severe malaria so easily in Nigeria?

options.A: Their immune defenses are either developing or temporarily lowered
options.B: They have a naturally higher body temperature that attracts vectors
options.C: They spend more time outdoors during peak sunlight hours
options.D: Their diets lack the specific nutrients required to fight protozoa

explanation: You got it! Little ones are still building their immune defenses, and pregnancy naturally lowers a woman's immune response for a bit, making them extra vulnerable.

question: What form of the malaria parasite does a mosquito first inject into a person?

options.A: Merozoites
options.B: Gametocytes
options.C: Zygotes
options.D: Sporozoites

explanation: Correct! Infected mosquitoes carry sporozoites in their salivary glands and inject them right into your skin and blood when they bite.

question: What happens inside red blood cells to cause those sudden, recurring fever spikes in malaria?

options.A: The rapid multiplication and bursting of red blood cells
options.B: The sudden drop in total white blood cell production
options.C: The allergic reaction to mosquito saliva in the skin
options.D: The physical blocking of large arteries in the heart

explanation: Well done! As the parasites multiply and burst out of red blood cells, they release toxins that trigger a sudden, intense fever.

question: Which sign tells you a patient has severe malaria instead of just uncomplicated malaria?

options.A: Impaired consciousness or coma
options.B: Loss of appetite
options.C: Mild intermittent headache
options.D: Low-grade joint pain

explanation: Spot on! Any sign of confusion, extreme weakness, or coma (cerebral malaria) means it's an emergency needing immediate inpatient care.

question: A patient comes to the clinic with a fever and headache, but is fully alert and able to swallow drugs. How do you classify this?

options.A: Asymptomatic malaria
options.B: Chronic malaria
options.C: Severe malaria
options.D: Uncomplicated malaria

explanation: Correct! Because the patient is stable and can take oral meds without danger signs, it's uncomplicated malaria. You'll see this a lot in clinical postings!

question: Why shouldn't nurses just give anti-malarials immediately to every patient with a fever without testing first?

options.A: RDT kits never work during the rainy season
options.B: Patients refuse to take medications without laboratory proof
options.C: Malaria drugs are too expensive to give out freely
options.D: Many other infections can cause similar symptoms to malaria

explanation: You got it! Illnesses like typhoid or UTIs can also cause fever. Testing first stops us from mistreating patients and wasting precious drugs.

question: What makes a Rapid Diagnostic Test (RDT) so great for a busy rural health clinic?

options.A: It gives quick results from a finger-prick blood sample without complex equipment
options.B: It permanently prevents future mosquito bites from causing infection
options.C: It is the only test capable of identifying dead parasites after treatment
options.D: It tells the nurse the exact number of parasites circulating in the blood

explanation: Spot on! RDTs are fast, portable, and a lifesaver in clinics where there are no fancy lab machines or steady electricity.

question: Why do we combine two different drugs in Artemisinin-Based Combination Therapy (ACT)?

options.A: To make the medication taste better for young children
options.B: To shorten the treatment duration to a single dose
options.C: To eliminate the need for any laboratory blood testing
options.D: To prevent or delay the development of parasite resistance

explanation: Correct! Teaming up two drugs with different actions helps wipe out all parasites cleanly and stops them from learning how to fight off the medicine.

question: A patient with severe malaria is admitted to your ward. How should they first receive their medication?

options.A: Oral tablets swallowed with water
options.B: Subcutaneous daily injection
options.C: Rectal suppositories only
options.D: Intravenous or intramuscular

explanation: Well done! Severe cases move fast, so we need fast-acting injections (IV or IM artesunate) to get the drug into their system immediately.

question: What is the main goal of Intermittent Preventive Treatment in pregnancy (IPTp)?

options.A: To prevent the woman from ever being bitten by a mosquito
options.B: To boost the production of red blood cells in the bone marrow
options.C: To cure a severe case of cerebral malaria in the third trimester
options.D: To clear hidden parasites and protect the mother and baby

explanation: Spot on! IPTp is given during antenatal care to keep pregnant mums and their babies safe from the hidden dangers of malaria.

question: Why are Insecticide-Treated Nets (ITNs) most effective when used while sleeping?

options.A: Anopheles mosquitoes bite mostly at night when people are asleep
options.B: It prevents mosquitoes from laying eggs inside household water pots
options.C: The chemical on the net repels daytime flies and cockroaches
options.D: It completely stops the flow of humid air into the bedroom

explanation: You got it! Since malaria mosquitoes love to hunt during the night, sleeping under a treated net hits them right when they are most active.

question: What causes severe anemia in a patient with advanced malaria?

options.A: A complete failure of dietary iron absorption in the gut
options.B: Sudden internal bleeding in the gastrointestinal tract
options.C: Suppression of kidney function leading to blood loss in urine
options.D: Destruction and rapid loss of red blood cells by the parasite

explanation: Correct! As the malaria parasites multiply and break open red blood cells en masse, the patient's blood count drops sharply, causing severe anemia.

question: An unconscious child with cerebral malaria is brought into the emergency ward. What is your very first nursing priority?

options.A: Ensuring a clear airway and monitoring breathing
options.B: Discharging the patient home with anti-malarial tablets
options.C: Encouraging the mother to feed the child oral porridge
options.D: Checking visual acuity using a Snellen eye chart

explanation: Spot on! ABCs come first in nursing. An unconscious child can easily choke or struggle to breathe, so keeping that airway open is priority number one.

question: How does health education in the community help reduce malaria cases?

options.A: It empowers families to use preventive tools and seek early testing
options.B: It replaces the need for hospital laboratories in rural zones
options.C: It provides immediate immunity to newborns in endemic regions
options.D: It permanently eliminates mosquito breeding sites nationwide

explanation: Well done! Teaching families how to use nets properly and report fevers early stops infections before they spiral out of control.

question: Which of these is NOT a standard community prevention message taught by nurses?

options.A: Attending antenatal clinics for preventive treatment during pregnancy
options.B: Sleeping inside insecticide-treated nets every single night
options.C: Taking high doses of antibiotics to prevent malaria infection
options.D: Clearing stagnant water puddles around residential houses

explanation: Correct! Antibiotics fight bacteria, not malaria parasites. Taking them for malaria is incorrect and only builds drug resistance.

question: What specific cells in the human body does HIV primarily attack and destroy?

options.A: CD4+ T-lymphocytes
options.B: Neutrophils
options.C: Red blood cells
options.D: Platelets

explanation: HIV specifically targets and destroys CD4+ T-lymphocytes, which weakens the immune response over time. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h1)

question: What is the main difference between HIV and AIDS?

options.A: HIV only affects children whereas AIDS affects adults.
options.B: HIV is transmitted by blood while AIDS is transmitted sexually.
options.C: AIDS can be cured completely with antibiotics unlike HIV.
options.D: AIDS is the advanced stage when the immune system is severely damaged.

explanation: Think of HIV as the virus that enters the body, and AIDS as the later stage when the immune system gets very weak and can no longer fight off sickness.

question: Which enzyme helps HIV convert its viral RNA into DNA inside the host cell?

options.A: Reverse transcriptase
options.B: Amylase
options.C: Pepsin
options.D: DNA polymerase

explanation: HIV uses an enzyme called reverse transcriptase to rewrite its genetic code from RNA into DNA so it can hide inside our body's cells. Clever little virus, but now you know its trick!

question: Which of the following is NOT a primary mode of HIV transmission?

options.A: Unprotected sexual intercourse with an infected person
options.B: Sharing contaminated needles among drug users
options.C: Casual social contact like hugging and sharing utensils
options.D: Transmission from an infected mother to her baby during birth

explanation: HIV is not spread through everyday casual social contact, sweat, tears, saliva, or insect bites. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h2)

question: What happens during the clinical latency stage of HIV?

options.A: The immune system completely eradicates the virus without treatment.
options.B: The virus multiplies slowly and the patient often feels healthy.
options.C: CD4 cell counts rapidly increase above normal levels.
options.D: The patient experiences severe opportunistic infections immediately.

explanation: During this quiet period, the virus stays active but multiplies slowly. Many patients look and feel completely fine, which is why testing is so important!

question: A patient is officially diagnosed with AIDS when their CD4 count drops below which threshold?

options.A: 800 cells/mm3
options.B: 200 cells/mm3
options.C: 500 cells/mm3
options.D: 1000 cells/mm3

explanation: A CD4 count falling below 200 cells/mm3 marks the transition from chronic HIV infection to a diagnosis of AIDS. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h3)

question: Within how many hours must Post-Exposure Prophylaxis (PEP) be started to work effectively?

options.A: 24 days
options.B: 1 week
options.C: 72 hours
options.D: 1 month

explanation: Time is precious here! PEP needs to start as soon as possible, and ideally within 72 hours after a possible exposure, to stop the virus from taking root.

question: How does Pre-Exposure Prophylaxis (PrEP) help prevent HIV?

options.A: It is given as a one-time vaccine to provide lifelong immunity.
options.B: It is taken only after a person knows they have been exposed to the virus.
options.C: It kills existing opportunistic infections in AIDS patients.
options.D: It is taken daily by HIV-negative people to block the virus from establishing an infection.

explanation: Think of PrEP as a daily shield. People who are HIV-negative take it regularly to keep the virus from setting up shop if exposure happens.

question: What does the acronym VCT stand for in HIV nursing care?

options.A: Vaccination and Chemotherapy Therapy
options.B: Voluntary Counseling and Testing
options.C: Viral Care Treatment
options.D: Venereal Control Technique

explanation: VCT stands for Voluntary Counseling and Testing, a core strategy for encouraging people to know their HIV status confidentially. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h5)

question: A patient tests positive for HIV at the clinic. What is your best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Report the patient's name to local community leaders immediately
options.B: Advise the patient to stop working and isolate at home forever
options.C: Provide compassionate post-test counseling and link the patient to treatment services
options.D: Wait until the patient asks questions before saying anything about treatment

explanation: A positive test can be scary. As a nurse, your warmth, privacy, and gentle guidance are vital to connect them straight to the care they need.

question: What is the main goal of Antiretroviral Therapy (ART)?

options.A: To suppress viral replication and reduce the viral load to undetectable levels
options.B: To prevent bacterial infections like pneumonia and tuberculosis
options.C: To completely eliminate the HIV virus from every cell in the body
options.D: To cure advanced stages of AIDS within two weeks of treatment

explanation: While ART doesn't clear every single trace of the virus, it puts a heavy brake on it, lowering the viral load so the immune system can bounce back and stay strong.

question: Why is taking ART medications every single day so important for patients?

options.A: Missing a single dose causes immediate death from opportunistic infections.
options.B: Inconsistent taking of drugs can cause the virus to mutate and develop resistance to treatment.
options.C: Taking pills at irregular times makes the medication taste much worse.
options.D: Strict adherence is only necessary during the first month of therapy.

explanation: Consistency is key! If a patient skips doses, drug levels drop in the blood, giving the crafty virus a chance to change its form and beat the medicine.

question: What does PMTCT stand for in maternal and child health nursing?

options.A: Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission
options.B: Primary Medical Treatment and Care Techniques
options.C: Pediatric Medication Testing and Clinical Trials
options.D: Post-Natal Maternal Complication Treatment

explanation: PMTCT stands for Prevention of Mother-to-Child Transmission, which encompasses strategies to stop vertical HIV spread during pregnancy, birth, and breastfeeding. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T4#GNS214_U1_T4_h7)

question: When should an HIV-positive pregnant woman start taking ART under PMTCT guidelines?

options.A: Only if she develops symptoms of full-blown AIDS
options.B: Immediately upon diagnosis, regardless of CD4 count
options.C: Only after the baby is successfully delivered
options.D: Only during the final month of pregnancy

explanation: Starting ART right away helps drop the mother's viral load as low as possible, giving her baby the best shield of protection before birth.

question: What is the most common opportunistic infection and leading cause of death in people with HIV?

options.A: Tetanus
options.B: Tuberculosis
options.C: Cholera
options.D: Malaria

explanation: Tuberculosis (TB) is the top opportunistic infection we watch out for in patients with weakened immune systems. Catching it early saves lives!

question: Why do patients with advanced HIV easily catch opportunistic infections?

options.A: Their red blood cell count drops too low to carry oxygen.
options.B: Antiretroviral medications cause bacterial infections as a side effect.
options.C: Their damaged immune systems cannot fight off germs that healthy bodies easily control.
options.D: They live in environments with too many synthetic chemicals.

explanation: When CD4 cells are low, the body's security guard is down. Germs that wouldn't normally bother a healthy person can easily cause trouble.

question: What is a major negative effect of HIV-related stigma in our communities?

options.A: It eliminates the need for VCT clinics.
options.B: It discourages people from getting tested or seeking treatment.
options.C: It increases the effectiveness of antiretroviral drugs.
options.D: It causes the HIV virus to mutate into a weaker strain.

explanation: Fear of being judged makes people hide their status and stay away from clinics. Compassion and education are our best tools to fight this stigma!

question: How do home-based care programs help patients with advanced HIV disease?

options.A: By diagnosing new infectious diseases without laboratory testing equipment
options.B: By replacing the need for antiretroviral medications entirely with herbal remedies
options.C: By providing family-supported nursing care, hygiene assistance, and monitoring at home
options.D: By isolating patients from their families so they never leave the bedroom

explanation: Home-based care brings comfort right to the doorstep, helping families manage daily nursing care, hygiene, and spotting any new symptoms early.

question: What is the primary causative organism of pulmonary tuberculosis?

options.A: Klebsiella pneumoniae
options.B: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.C: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.D: Staphylococcus aureus

explanation: Pulmonary tuberculosis is specifically caused by the rod-shaped bacterium called Mycobacterium tuberculosis. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T5#GNS214_U1_T5_h1)

question: What is the main difference between latent TB and active TB disease?

options.A: Latent TB bacteria are dead, while active TB bacteria are alive.
options.B: Latent TB requires hospital admission, while active TB is treated at home.
options.C: Latent TB only affects children, while active TB only affects adults.
options.D: Latent TB has no symptoms and is not contagious, whereas active TB causes illness and spreads.

explanation: Think of latent TB as sleeping quietly in the body—the person feels fine and cannot pass it on. Active TB is awake, causing illness, and can spread to others.

question: How does pulmonary tuberculosis usually spread from one person to another?

options.A: By sharing eating utensils
options.B: Through direct skin-to-skin contact
options.C: Through contaminated drinking water
options.D: By airborne droplet nuclei

explanation: TB travels through tiny droplets in the air when someone with active TB coughs or sneezes. That's why breathing the same enclosed air can lead to infection.

question: Why do poorly ventilated and overcrowded rooms make the spread of TB worse?

options.A: They trap airborne droplet nuclei and keep concentrations high.
options.B: They weaken human skin barriers against germs.
options.C: They lower the room temperature and freeze the bacteria.
options.D: They cause people to share contaminated food items.

explanation: Without fresh air moving in and out, infectious droplets just hang around in the room, making it much easier for someone nearby to breathe them in.

question: What is the protective little wall of cells that the immune system builds around TB bacteria called?

options.A: Abscess
options.B: Hematoma
options.C: Aneurysm
options.D: Granuloma

explanation: Your immune system tries to trap the germs by building a wall of cells around them. This little cluster is called a granuloma or tubercle.

question: What happens right in the center of an old TB tubercle as the infection sits there?

options.A: Caseous necrosis or cheese-like tissue death
options.B: Conversion of bacteria into normal flora
options.C: Rapid regeneration of healthy lung tissue
options.D: Calcification into solid bone-like structures

explanation: As the battle inside the tubercle continues, the center part of the tissue dies and turns into a soft, crumbly substance that looks a bit like cheese—hence 'caseous necrosis'.

question: What is the medical term for coughing up blood-stained sputum?

options.A: Hemoptysis
options.B: Melena
options.C: Hematemesis
options.D: Epistaxis

explanation: Coughing up blood from the lungs is called hemoptysis. It's one of those classic signs in clinical wards that always catches a nurse's attention!

question: A patient comes to the clinic with a cough lasting four weeks, drenching night sweats, and sudden weight loss. What should you suspect first?

options.A: Acute tension headache
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Simple seasonal allergy
options.D: Pulmonary tuberculosis

explanation: A long-standing cough, night sweats, and dropping weight without trying form the classic triad for active pulmonary TB. Great clinical spotting!

question: Which laboratory stain is used to spot tuberculosis bacteria under the microscope?

options.A: Wright stain
options.B: Methylene blue stain
options.C: Gram stain
options.D: Ziehl-Neelsen stain

explanation: TB bugs are stubborn 'acid-fast' bacteria, so we use the Ziehl-Neelsen stain to make them pop out brightly under the microscope.

question: What is the big advantage of using rapid molecular tests like GeneXpert for TB?

options.A: They replace the need for taking a thorough patient history.
options.B: They provide fast results and detect drug resistance early.
options.C: They can cure the infection without any medications.
options.D: They are completely painless and require no patient samples.

explanation: GeneXpert is fantastic because it gives results in just a few hours and tells us right away if the drugs won't work against that specific strain.

question: What is the main goal of the DOTS (Directly Observed Therapy Short-Course) program?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of manufacturing TB drugs
options.B: To eliminate the need for sputum microscopy tests
options.C: To force patients to stay admitted in the hospital for six months
options.D: To ensure patients swallow every dose of medicine to prevent drug resistance

explanation: With DOTS, a health worker watches the patient take their medication. This makes sure they finish the course and stops drug-resistant TB from developing.

question: Why do we treat active tuberculosis with multiple drugs instead of just one antibiotic?

options.A: It makes the treatment course last much longer.
options.B: It eliminates the need for any nutritional support.
options.C: It lowers the risk of common stomach upsets.
options.D: It prevents the bacteria from easily developing drug resistance.

explanation: Hitting the TB bacteria with a combination of strong drugs makes it nearly impossible for the germs to mutate and outsmart the treatment.

question: Which vaccine is routinely given to newborns to protect against severe forms of childhood TB?

options.A: OPV vaccine
options.B: BCG vaccine
options.C: MMR vaccine
options.D: Tetanus toxoid

explanation: The BCG vaccine is given early in life to give babies strong backup against the most dangerous, widespread forms of childhood TB.

question: Which of these is NOT a correct infection control step when nursing a patient with active TB?

options.A: Ensuring nurses wear fitted N95 respirator masks
options.B: Placing the patient in an airborne infection isolation room
options.C: Instructing the patient to cover their mouth when coughing
options.D: Keeping the patient's room doors and windows tightly sealed shut from fresh air

explanation: Sealing a room shut traps the infectious germs inside! We always need good ventilation or negative pressure to clear out the air safely.

question: What major organ side effect must nurses watch out for when patients take drugs like isoniazid and rifampicin?

options.A: Liver toxicity or hepatotoxicity
options.B: Sudden bone fractures
options.C: Permanent kidney failure
options.D: Complete hair loss

explanation: First-line TB drugs are processed by the liver, so nurses must monitor closely for signs of liver stress or toxicity.

question: A patient taking ethambutol reports noticing a change in their vision. What should you do first?

options.A: Report the visual changes promptly to the prescriber.
options.B: Double the next dose of the medication.
options.C: Advise the patient to stop eating green vegetables.
options.D: Reassure the patient that blurry vision is a normal temporary sign.

explanation: Ethambutol can affect the eyes (optic neuritis). Any vision changes need a quick report to the doctor so we can protect the patient's sight!

question: What is another name commonly used for leprosy?

options.A: Bright's disease
options.B: Lyme disease
options.C: Hansen's disease
options.D: Koch's disease

explanation: Leprosy is also called Hansen's disease, named after the scientist who discovered the causative bacterium. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T6#GNS214_U1_T6_h1)

question: Which parts of the body are mainly affected by leprosy?

options.A: Bones and joints
options.B: Liver and gut
options.C: Skin and peripheral nerves
options.D: Lungs and upper airways

explanation: The leprosy bacteria love cooler areas of the body, which is why they mainly attack the skin and the nerves outside the brain and spinal cord. You've got this!

question: What is the name of the bacterium that causes leprosy?

options.A: Mycobacterium tuberculosis
options.B: Streptococcus pneumoniae
options.C: Plasmodium falciparum
options.D: Mycobacterium leprae

explanation: Mycobacterium leprae is the specific acid-fast bacillus responsible for causing leprosy. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T6#GNS214_U1_T6_h2)

question: Why is it often hard to tell exactly when someone caught leprosy?

options.A: It takes a very long time for signs to show up
options.B: Early symptoms always go away on their own
options.C: It spreads through dirty drinking water
options.D: The bacteria die instantly outside the body

explanation: Because symptoms can take months or even years to appear, it is tough to trace back the exact moment of exposure. Don't worry, you're learning!

question: What is the highest number of skin patches a patient can have to be classified as having paucibacillary leprosy?

options.A: 2 patches
options.B: 20 patches
options.C: 5 patches
options.D: 10 patches

explanation: Paucibacillary simply means 'few bacteria.' Clinically, it's marked by having between one and five skin patches. You're doing great!

question: What main factor decides if a patient develops mild (paucibacillary) or severe (multibacillary) leprosy?

options.A: The local water supply
options.B: The person's age when infected
options.C: The country where exposure happened
options.D: The strength of the patient's immune system

explanation: It all comes down to how well the body's immune system fights off the bacteria. A stronger defense means fewer lesions! You're getting the hang of this.

question: What is usually the very first sign of leprosy on the skin?

options.A: A discolored patch that feels numb or less sensitive
options.B: Tiny water blisters on the hands
options.C: Painful open sores on the legs
options.D: Severe itching all over the body

explanation: A pale or reddish skin patch that doesn't feel normal touch or temperature is the classic early warning sign. Keep shining!

question: A patient comes in with a swollen ulnar nerve and a numb patch on the arm. What should you suspect?

options.A: High blood pressure
options.B: A normal heat rash
options.C: Low blood levels (anemia)
options.D: Leprosy

explanation: When a nerve is thickened and a skin patch loses its feeling, leprosy should immediately come to mind. Spotting these clues makes you a great nurse!

question: Why do leprosy patients often end up with serious sores on their hands and feet?

options.A: Unbearable itching makes them scratch too hard
options.B: Blood completely stops flowing to the fingers and toes
options.C: Loss of feeling causes them to injure themselves without knowing
options.D: Bacteria directly dissolve the skin cells

explanation: Because they can't feel pain, heat, or sharp objects, minor cuts go unnoticed and turn into nasty ulcers. You're building solid clinical instincts!

question: Which facial nerve problem puts a leprosy patient at risk of going blind?

options.A: Bell's palsy
options.B: Lagophthalmos
options.C: Jaw nerve pain
options.D: Facial drooping

explanation: Lagophthalmos means the patient can't close their eyes fully. This leaves the eyeball dry and prone to damage. You're mastering clinical terms step by step!

question: Why is leprosy treated with a mix of different drugs instead of just one?

options.A: To cut out the need for blood tests
options.B: To heal skin sores overnight
options.C: To stop the bacteria from becoming resistant to the drugs
options.D: To make the treatment cheaper to buy

explanation: Using a combination of medications ensures the smart little germs can't mutate and outsmart a single drug. Brilliant concept to know!

question: How long is the standard course of multi-drug therapy for a patient with multibacillary leprosy?

options.A: Exactly 6 months
options.B: 6 weeks
options.C: 3 to 5 years
options.D: 12 to 24 months

explanation: Multibacillary cases require a longer treatment duration, usually lasting 12 to 24 months, to clear the higher bacterial load. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T6#GNS214_U1_T6_h6)

question: What is a very important self-care habit to teach a patient who cannot feel their feet?

options.A: Washing with harsh antiseptic spirit daily
options.B: Checking the feet every single day for cuts and sores
options.C: Walking barefoot to make the soles tougher
options.D: Soaking feet in hot water to boost blood flow

explanation: Since they won't feel pain from a thorn or scrape, daily mirror checks help catch injuries before they turn into bad ulcers. You are learning real patient care!

question: A recovering leprosy patient feels very depressed because people in the community are avoiding them. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Advise them to pack up and relocate to another state
options.B: Assure them that people will soon forget about it
options.C: Offer a listening ear and connect them with a support group
options.D: Tell the patient never to discuss their illness with anyone

explanation: Emotional support and connecting with others who understand are powerful ways to beat stigma and heal the mind. You're going to be a wonderfully empathetic nurse!

question: What is the main public health step used to stop leprosy from spreading in a town or village?

options.A: Finding cases early and starting treatment right away
options.B: Washing living areas with heavy chemicals
options.C: Locking all infected people away in isolated camps
options.D: Giving mandatory vaccines to every newborn baby

explanation: Catching cases early and starting medications quickly stops the spread because treatment makes patients non-infectious! Public health in action!

question: Why do community health nurses keep a close eye on people living in the same house as a leprosy patient?

options.A: They are forced to pay for the patient's hospital bills
options.B: They are at higher risk because they spend so much time together
options.C: They are legally banned from leaving the house during treatment
options.D: They must swallow preventive antibiotics for years

explanation: Living closely under one roof means more exposure time, so checking family members regularly helps catch any early signs. Fantastic job completing this set!

question: What is the common name for onchocerciasis?

options.A: Sleeping sickness
options.B: River blindness
options.C: Elephantiasis
options.D: Swamp fever

explanation: Onchocerciasis is widely known as river blindness because the blackfly vectors breed near fast-flowing rivers where transmission is highest. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T7#GNS214_U1_T7_h1)

question: Which insect transmits the parasite that causes onchocerciasis to humans?

options.A: Simulium blackfly
options.B: Tsetse fly
options.C: Sandfly
options.D: Anopheles mosquito

explanation: The female Simulium blackfly is the vector here. She loves fast-flowing rivers, which is how the infection spreads in endemic rural areas.

question: What are the tiny, baby worms produced by adult Onchocerca volvulus called?

options.A: Sporozoites
options.B: Trophozoites
options.C: Cercariae
options.D: Microfilariae

explanation: Spot on! The adult female worms release millions of microfilariae, which then travel through the skin and eye tissues, causing those troublesome symptoms.

question: Where do microfilariae mainly travel and live in the human body?

options.A: Inside liver tissue permanently
options.B: Major arteries only
options.C: Skin and subcutaneous tissues
options.D: Cerebrospinal fluid

explanation: Unlike some parasites that hang out strictly in the blood, these little ones love to migrate through your skin and tissues, setting off local immune reactions.

question: What skin changes usually show up in long-term onchocerciasis?

options.A: Bright red circular rashes
options.B: Widespread skin bruising
options.C: Severe itching and skin thickening
options.D: Painful pus-filled blisters

explanation: Chronic infections cause intense itching. Over time, all that scratching leads to thickened skin with a texture people sometimes compare to lizard skin.

question: A patient near a fast-flowing river has firm, painless lumps over their hip bones and very itchy skin. What is the most likely condition?

options.A: Acute appendicitis
options.B: Iron deficiency anemia
options.C: Onchocerciasis
options.D: Malaria

explanation: You've got it! Those painless lumps (nodules) over bony areas combined with terrible itching near a river are classic signs of river blindness.

question: What is the standard diagnostic test used to confirm onchocerciasis?

options.A: Chest X-ray imaging
options.B: Bone marrow biopsy
options.C: Stool microscopy for ova
options.D: Skin snip microscopy

explanation: Taking small skin snips and observing the crawling microfilariae under a microscope remains the standard diagnostic method. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T7#GNS214_U1_T7_h4)

question: Why aren't standard antibody blood tests ideal for diagnosing an active case of onchocerciasis?

options.A: They only work during the first week of a bite
options.B: They require frozen tissue samples to function
options.C: They show past exposure rather than current infection
options.D: They cannot detect any immune response in humans

explanation: Antibodies stick around in the blood long after the body has dealt with the parasite. A positive blood test just means past exposure, not necessarily an active worm load right now.

question: Which medication is the main choice for treating onchocerciasis?

options.A: Ivermectin
options.B: Penicillin
options.C: Chloroquine
options.D: Quinine

explanation: Ivermectin is the superstar drug used worldwide to clear out microfilariae and protect people's sight.

question: What causes the Mazzotti reaction when treating an onchocerciasis patient?

options.A: The rapid immune reaction to dying microfilariae
options.B: Complete failure of the patient's liver and kidneys
options.C: Bacterial superinfection in the skin snip sites
options.D: A direct toxic allergic reaction to the drug capsule

explanation: When ivermectin kills thousands of microfilariae all at once, the sudden immune system cleanup causes fever, rash, and swelling known as the Mazzotti reaction.

question: What is the main public health strategy used worldwide to wipe out onchocerciasis?

options.A: Mass vaccination campaigns with live attenuated virus
options.B: Daily antibiotic prophylaxis for all infants
options.C: Community-directed treatment with ivermectin
options.D: Complete relocation of riverbank settlements

explanation: Giving out ivermectin yearly through community-led programs breaks the transmission cycle and protects village vision.

question: A community health nurse is planning care in a village near a fast-flowing river. Which action best supports primary prevention?

options.A: Isolating infected patients in hospital wards for six months
options.B: Administering daily eye drops to every school-aged child
options.C: Educating residents on wearing protective clothing and using ivermectin
options.D: Surgically removing all subcutaneous nodules from every villager

explanation: Teaching folks how to avoid blackfly bites and combining that with community ivermectin distribution is the gold standard in public health nursing.

question: What is the most serious and permanent complication of untreated onchocerciasis?

options.A: Blindness
options.B: Paraplegia
options.C: Deafness
options.D: Kidney failure

explanation: Long-term eye inflammation from dying microfilariae eventually scars the eye tissue, leading to irreversible river blindness if left untreated.

question: Why does untreated onchocerciasis heavily hurt the economy of rural farming communities?

options.A: Infected workers require lifelong confinement in institutions
options.B: Governments ban all agricultural exports from endemic zones
options.C: Vision loss and chronic pain prevent adults from farming
options.D: The disease infects livestock and destroys local crop yields

explanation: When adults lose their sight or suffer from debilitating skin pain, they can no longer farm. This hits family income and rural food production hard.

question: When do Lassa fever outbreaks usually peak in Nigeria?

options.A: November to May
options.B: Throughout the entire year equally
options.C: September to October
options.D: June to August

explanation: You'll see more cases during the dry season. Bush burning and farming drive rodents closer to human homes looking for food and shelter.

question: Why does Lassa fever spike during the dry season?

options.A: Farming activities and bush burning drive rats closer to homes
options.B: Cold weather lowers human immune systems significantly
options.C: Increased humidity allows the virus to spread faster in the air
options.D: Heavy rainfall causes stagnant water to breed the virus

explanation: When fields are cleared and burned, the rats lose their natural habitat and move straight into grain stores and residential areas.

question: Which animal is the main carrier of the Lassa virus?

options.A: Domestic house cat
options.B: Mastomys rat
options.C: Ground squirrel
options.D: Fruit bat

explanation: The multimammate rat (Mastomys species) is the natural reservoir that carries and spreads the virus without getting sick itself.

question: How do Mastomys rats spread the Lassa virus around?

options.A: By biting humans aggressively during daylight hours
options.B: By carrying ticks that drop onto human skin
options.C: By shedding the virus in their urine, faeces, and saliva
options.D: Through respiratory droplets when they sneeze or cough

explanation: Even though the rats don't look sick, their droppings and urine constantly contaminate food items and household surfaces.

question: What is the most common way people first catch Lassa fever?

options.A: Being bitten by infected mosquitoes at dusk
options.B: Swimming in slow-moving rural rivers
options.C: Eating food contaminated by rat urine or faeces
options.D: Inhaling dust from sweeping dry sandy floors

explanation: Ingesting food or water touched by infected rodent waste is the number one way the virus enters the human body.

question: Who is at the highest risk of catching Lassa fever in a hospital?

options.A: A nurse caring for a bleeding patient without proper personal protective equipment
options.B: A pharmacist dispensing oral medications from a secure dispensary
options.C: A patient admitted to the medical ward for severe malaria
options.D: A visitor sitting quietly across the room from a stable patient

explanation: Direct contact with infectious body fluids like blood without barrier protection puts healthcare workers at serious risk.

question: What is a well-known long-term issue for people who survive Lassa fever?

options.A: Loss of vision
options.B: Chronic kidney failure
options.C: Deafness
options.D: Permanent limb paralysis

explanation: Hearing loss is quite common after recovering from Lassa fever, and unfortunately, it can sometimes be permanent.

question: Which part of the body takes the hardest hit, leading to shock in Lassa fever?

options.A: Blood vessels and endothelial lining
options.B: Peripheral nervous system
options.C: Upper respiratory airways
options.D: Skeletal muscle tissue

explanation: The virus attacks the lining of blood vessels, causing fluid to leak out of capillaries, which can rapidly lead to shock.

question: Why is it so tricky to diagnose Lassa fever early just by looking at symptoms?

options.A: Patients rarely present with any fever during the first week
options.B: Its early symptoms closely resemble malaria and typhoid fever
options.C: Skin rashes appear immediately to confuse the clinician
options.D: Laboratory tests are always positive within the first two hours

explanation: Fever, headache, and body weakness happen with many tropical illnesses, which is why taking a careful travel and exposure history is so important.

question: Which lab test is most commonly used to confirm a Lassa virus infection?

options.A: Microscopic stool examination for ova
options.B: Sputum acid-fast bacilli smear
options.C: Electrocardiogram rhythm strip
options.D: Reverse Transcription-Polymerase Chain Reaction (RT-PCR)

explanation: RT-PCR checks for viral RNA in the blood with great accuracy, making it the gold standard for confirmation.

question: What is the main antiviral drug used to treat Lassa fever?

options.A: Chloroquine
options.B: Ribavirin
options.C: Artemether
options.D: Acyclovir

explanation: Ribavirin is the go-to antiviral. When given early, it drastically lowers the severity of the illness and saves lives.

question: When does antiviral treatment work best for a Lassa fever patient?

options.A: After all laboratory confirmation test results return
options.B: During the convalescent recovery phase
options.C: Within the first six days of symptom onset
options.D: Only after the patient develops bleeding from the gums

explanation: Catching it early stops the virus from multiplying wildly before it causes severe organ damage.

question: A Lassa fever patient's urine output drops to 15 mL/hour over two hours. What should you do first?

options.A: Document the finding as normal for viral infections and recheck in eight hours
options.B: Encourage the patient to drink large volumes of plain water quickly
options.C: Stop all intravenous fluid infusions to give the kidneys a rest
options.D: Notify the doctor immediately and assess for developing kidney compromise

explanation: Low urine output is a red flag for acute kidney injury. Always report it promptly so the medical team can adjust care.

question: Why is keeping a strict fluid balance chart so vital for a Lassa fever patient?

options.A: To prevent both dehydration and dangerous fluid overload leading to pulmonary edema
options.B: To calculate the exact amount of oral medication required daily
options.C: To ensure the patient loses weight while admitted in the isolation ward
options.D: To test the concentration of protein present in the blood plasma

explanation: Because leaky blood vessels make fluid management tricky, too little fluid causes shock, while too much fills the lungs.

question: Which infection control step is absolutely mandatory when nursing a suspected Lassa fever patient?

options.A: Placing every patient in a carpeted, air-conditioned room
options.B: Allowing family members to wash the patient's soiled linens
options.C: Using full personal protective equipment and barrier nursing
options.D: Administering prophylactic antibiotics to all hospital visitors

explanation: Barrier nursing with full PPE is non-negotiable to keep infectious body fluids away from staff and other patients.

question: Why shouldn't healthcare workers hand-wash contaminated Lassa patient linens in open basins?

options.A: Modern detergents are too expensive for primary clinics
options.B: It risks splashing infectious bodily fluids and spreading the virus
options.C: Washing powder damages the fabric of hospital bedsheets
options.D: Soap destroys the color of standard hospital linen sets

explanation: Washing linen by hand in open spaces creates splashes and mists that can expose staff to dangerous viral particles.

question: What is a key prevention message nurses should teach families to stop Lassa fever at home?

options.A: Keep doors and windows wide open during the evening hours
options.B: Dry all harvested grains directly on bare soil surfaces
options.C: Store food items in tightly sealed, rodent-proof containers
options.D: Keep pet cats away from all residential cooking areas

explanation: Locking up food in secure containers keeps rats away and stops them from contaminating your grains with urine and faeces.

question: How do disease tracking and early reporting help control Lassa fever outbreaks?

options.A: They guarantee that no new rats will enter the village boundaries
options.B: They eliminate the need for expensive antiviral medications in clinics
options.C: They allow quick isolation and treatment of cases before the virus spreads further
options.D: They prevent the dry season weather from occurring each year

explanation: Catching and isolating cases early breaks the chain of transmission, keeping families and communities safe.

question: What type of organism causes yellow fever?

options.A: A protozoan
options.B: A bacterium
options.C: A virus
options.D: A fungus

explanation: Yellow fever is an acute viral disease caused by a member of the Flaviviridae family. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h1)

question: Why are yellow fever outbreaks common in tropical places like Nigeria?

options.A: Climatic conditions strongly favor mosquito vector breeding and survival
options.B: The virus spreads directly from person to person through respiratory droplets
options.C: Local water treatment plants fail to kill the virus in drinking supplies
options.D: Wild animals migrate through cities and drop the virus into food markets

explanation: You got this! Warm, humid weather is just what Aedes mosquitoes love, helping them breed quickly and spread the virus. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h1)

question: Which insect is the main carrier that spreads yellow fever in towns and cities?

options.A: Tsetse fly
options.B: Aedes aegypti mosquito
options.C: House fly
options.D: Anopheles mosquito

explanation: Great job! The Aedes aegypti mosquito lives close to human homes, making it the primary villain in spreading urban yellow fever. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h2)

question: How does yellow fever pass from one person to another?

options.A: By direct skin contact with the sweat or saliva of a carrier
options.B: By sharing eating utensils or drinking cups with an infected individual
options.C: Through the bite of an infected mosquito that previously bit a sick person
options.D: Through airborne droplets released when a patient coughs or sneezes

explanation: Spot on! Yellow fever needs a mosquito middleman—you cannot catch it just by touching or breathing near someone who is sick. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h2)

question: What is the name of the middle phase of yellow fever when a patient's early symptoms temporarily disappear?

options.A: Convalescent phase
options.B: Remission phase
options.C: Intoxication phase
options.D: Viremic phase

explanation: That's correct! During the remission phase, the patient might feel like they are magically getting better before any severe symptoms hit. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h3)

question: When a yellow fever patient enters the dangerous intoxication phase, which organs take the hardest hit?

options.A: Skin and joints
options.B: Liver and kidneys
options.C: Lungs and brain
options.D: Heart and pancreas

explanation: Well done! This severe stage targets vital internal organs, especially the liver (causing the yellow eyes) and the kidneys. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h3)

question: Which classic body sign gives yellow fever its name?

options.A: Cyanosis
options.B: Jaundice
options.C: Erythema
options.D: Pallor

explanation: Exactly! Liver trouble causes jaundice—a yellowing of the skin and eyes—which inspired the illness's name. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h4)

question: A patient with yellow fever vomits dark, coffee-ground looking material. What is this classic clinical sign called?

options.A: Melena stool
options.B: Gastric sludge
options.C: Biliary reflux
options.D: Black vomit

explanation: Spot on! Bleeding inside the stomach mixing with digestive acids produces the famous 'black vomit' seen in severe cases. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h4)

question: What is Faget's sign, a unique finding nurses watch for in yellow fever patients?

options.A: A slow pulse rate despite a high body temperature
options.B: A sudden drop in blood pressure accompanied by rapid breathing
options.C: A high fever that peaks only during evening hours
options.D: An irregular heart rhythm during the remission phase

explanation: You nailed it! Usually, fever makes the heart race, but Faget's sign is this quirky mismatch where the pulse stays surprisingly slow even with a high temperature. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h5)

question: As a nurse caring for a yellow fever patient, which action is most critical to prioritize?

options.A: Administering routine oral iron supplements
options.B: Monitoring strict fluid intake and output
options.C: Encouraging high ambulation in the hallways
options.D: Applying cold water packs to the skin continuously

explanation: Brilliant! Because kidney failure can sneak up fast, tracking what goes in and out helps you catch trouble early. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h5)

question: Why must nurses strictly avoid giving aspirin or ibuprofen to a yellow fever patient?

options.A: They cause the body temperature to spike dangerously high
options.B: They increase the risk of severe bleeding and hemorrhage
options.C: They destroy remaining healthy cells in the liver and kidneys
options.D: They neutralize the effectiveness of prescribed intravenous fluids

explanation: That's right! Yellow fever messes with normal blood clotting, and drugs like ibuprofen make bleeding way worse. Always check before giving pain meds! [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h6)

question: What is the main focus of medical treatment for someone sick with yellow fever?

options.A: Providing supportive care to manage symptoms and organ failure
options.B: Giving heavy doses of antibiotics to prevent secondary bacterial infections
options.C: Performing emergency surgery to remove the infected liver tissue
options.D: Administering a specific antiviral drug to destroy the virus quickly

explanation: Correct! Since there's no magic cure pill for the virus yet, treatment is all about supporting the patient's body until they fight it off. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h6)

question: At what age do infants in Nigeria routinely receive the yellow fever vaccine?

options.A: At nine months of age
options.B: At eighteen months of age
options.C: At six weeks of age
options.D: At birth before discharge

explanation: Spot on! The immunisation schedule gives the yellow fever shot right at nine months, paired with the measles vaccine. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h7)

question: How soon after getting the yellow fever vaccine does protective immunity usually kick in?

options.A: After three to six weeks
options.B: Only after a second booster dose
options.C: Within ten days
options.D: Immediately within minutes

explanation: Great work! The body builds up defenses quickly, giving solid protection within about ten days of getting the jab. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h7)

question: What is the main goal of disease surveillance at local health centers during an outbreak?

options.A: To treat water supply dams with heavy chemical disinfectants
options.B: To detect suspected cases early and prevent widespread transmission
options.C: To test every healthy citizen in the town for virus antibodies
options.D: To force all community members to stay indoors under quarantine

explanation: Exactly! Spotting sick people early lets healthcare teams jump in fast and stop the outbreak from spreading. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h8)

question: As a community health nurse, you notice several villagers showing signs of fever and yellow eyes. What is your best immediate action?

options.A: Report the cluster to local public health authorities for investigation
options.B: Distribute mosquito repellent creams without informing the government
options.C: Advise villagers to wait two weeks to see if symptoms disappear
options.D: Close down all local markets and schools in the affected region

explanation: You're a star! Always report unusual clusters of disease right away so public health teams can step in and protect the whole community. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T9#GNS214_U1_T9_h8)

question: What is the main goal of Maternal and Child Health (MCH) services?

options.A: To provide free surgical procedures for aging populations
options.B: To reduce preventable illness and death in mothers and children
options.C: To manage chronic diseases in older adults
options.D: To replace traditional birth practices completely

explanation: You got this! MCH services are specially designed to protect and support the health and survival of mothers and young children. Every win starts with knowing your core goal!

question: Why do we focus more on prevention than cure in MCH programs?

options.A: Preventive care stops complications before they become life-threatening
options.B: Curative care requires expensive machinery that is always unavailable
options.C: Curative care is prohibited in primary health care clinics
options.D: Preventive care completely eliminates the need for any medications

explanation: Spot-on! Stopping an illness before it takes root saves lives and energy compared to fighting an advanced disease later on. Prevention is your best tool as a nurse.

question: Which injection is routinely given during antenatal care to protect the newborn from tetanus?

options.A: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
options.B: Tetanus toxoid vaccine
options.C: Iron and folic acid tablets
options.D: Antimalarial drugs

explanation: Wonderful! Giving the tetanus toxoid vaccine to pregnant women helps build immunity that passes straight to the baby, keeping neonatal tetanus away.

question: Why must pregnant women attend antenatal clinics even when they feel completely fine?

options.A: Pregnant women are legally required to visit the clinic every single week
options.B: It is impossible to eat a balanced diet without clinic supervision
options.C: Clinics require attendance records to secure international funding
options.D: Dangerous conditions like high blood pressure can develop without early warning signs

explanation: Exactly! Silent issues like pre-eclampsia or anemia can build up inside without any obvious signs at first. Routine checks keep both mum and baby safe.

question: When is the best time to put a newborn baby to the breast for the very first time?

options.A: Only when the mother's milk turns white
options.B: After twenty-four hours of observation
options.C: Within the first hour after birth
options.D: Once the baby cries continuously

explanation: You nailed it! Starting breastfeeding within that first hour helps boost milk flow and gives the baby that precious, protective colostrum.

question: A new mother looks pale, feels dizzy, and her pad is soaked with bright red blood within 20 minutes. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Assess the uterine fundus for tone and massage if boggy
options.B: Wait until the scheduled six-week postnatal checkup
options.C: Tell the mother to walk around the room to improve circulation
options.D: Encourage the mother to drink large volumes of cold water

explanation: Great clinical thinking! These are classic signs of postpartum hemorrhage. Checking and massaging the uterus helps it contract and stops the bleeding.

question: What is the main reason for plotting a child's weight on a growth chart during clinic visits?

options.A: To check if the child needs immediate dental surgery
options.B: To calculate the exact adult height of the child
options.C: To determine how much money the family earns
options.D: To detect faltering growth early before severe malnutrition develops

explanation: Spot on! Growth charts let us catch weight drops or slow growth early so we can step in long before severe malnutrition sets in.

question: Why do nurses track developmental milestones like sitting up and walking in toddlers?

options.A: It determines when the child can stop receiving immunizations
options.B: It proves the child will excel academically in primary school
options.C: Milestones are only used for research and have no clinical value
options.D: Delays can signal underlying neurological, nutritional, or systemic problems

explanation: You got it! Tracking milestones helps you spot delays early so the child can get the right medical help or therapy quickly.

question: Why is maintaining the cold chain so important in immunization programs?

options.A: To keep vaccines potent and effective until administration
options.B: To prevent the clinic refrigerator from overheating
options.C: To freeze liquid vaccines into solid blocks
options.D: To make the vaccines easier to draw into a syringe

explanation: Brilliant! Vaccines are delicate biological products. If they get too warm, they lose their power to protect children against diseases.

question: Which of the following is NOT a goal of the Expanded Programme on Immunization (EPI)?

options.A: Reducing childhood mortality rates across the country
options.B: Protecting infants from vaccine-preventable infectious diseases
options.C: Completely eliminating all chronic genetic disorders in children
options.D: Building community immunity against dangerous pathogens

explanation: Correct! EPI focuses on infectious, vaccine-preventable diseases. Genetic disorders are inherited and aren't targeted by standard immunization vaccines.

question: What is the main advantage of using the IMCI strategy when treating sick children?

options.A: It looks at the whole child and evaluates multiple overlapping symptoms
options.B: It focuses exclusively on treating severe surgical emergencies
options.C: It replaces the need for any laboratory testing in rural clinics
options.D: It removes the need for nurses to talk with caregivers

explanation: You're doing great! IMCI helps you assess the whole child because sick kids often suffer from more than one issue at the same time.

question: A mother brings in her infant who is very sleepy (lethargic) and vomiting everything she feeds her. According to IMCI, what do these signs mean?

options.A: Normal infant behavior during a mild growth spurt
options.B: Minor symptoms that can be treated at home with rest
options.C: Side effects of routine immunization that need no action
options.D: General danger signs requiring urgent hospital referral

explanation: Spot on! Lethargy and inability to keep fluids down are red-flag danger signs. They mean the baby needs emergency hospital care right away.

question: What is the recommended minimum time gap between pregnancies to protect mum and baby?

options.A: Twelve weeks
options.B: At least twenty-four months
options.C: Six months
options.D: Five years

explanation: Wonderful! Waiting at least two years lets the mother recover her strength and nutrient stores, giving the next baby a healthier start.

question: Why is a mother's nutrition directly linked to her baby's health?

options.A: Nutritional deficiencies only affect the mother's hair and skin
options.B: Poor maternal nutrition often results in low birth weight and developmental challenges
options.C: Infants do not depend on maternal nutrient stores during pregnancy
options.D: A mother's diet has no effect on the fetus once the placenta forms

explanation: Exactly! The growing baby relies entirely on the mother for building blocks, making good maternal nutrition vital for proper growth.

question: What is a major role of Community Health Workers in maternal and child health?

options.A: Replacing professional nurses entirely in district hospitals
options.B: Conducting household visits and referring clients with danger signs to clinics
options.C: Importing foreign medical equipment for government clinics
options.D: Performing complex major surgeries in rural health posts

explanation: You got it! Community health workers bridge the gap by visiting homes, sharing health tips, and sending anyone with danger signs straight to the clinic.

question: Why is it important to involve traditional leaders and local birth attendants in primary health care?

options.A: They hold significant influence over community beliefs and healthcare-seeking behaviors
options.B: They are responsible for funding all primary health care clinics
options.C: They possess advanced medical degrees recognized by the nursing council
options.D: They act as legal inspectors of government health budgets

explanation: Brilliant! When respected local leaders are on board, community members are much more likely to trust nurses and use clinic services.

question: What is the primary focus of safe motherhood initiatives?

options.A: Ensuring a healthy pregnancy and safe childbirth for every woman
options.B: Providing free formula feeding to all newborns
options.C: Increasing the birth rate in rural communities
options.D: Eliminating the need for traditional birth attendants

explanation: Safe motherhood focuses directly on the health and survival of women throughout pregnancy, delivery, and the postpartum period. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h1)

question: Why does safe motherhood include mental and social well-being alongside physical health?

options.A: Because total health affects a woman's ability to care for herself and her baby
options.B: Because mental health issues only occur after delivery
options.C: Because physical health cannot be measured during pregnancy
options.D: Because social status is the only cause of maternal mortality

explanation: A holistic view of health recognizes that emotional and social support are just as vital as physical care for a mother and her child. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h1)

question: Which of the following is one of the core pillars of safe motherhood?

options.A: Mandatory caesarean sections
options.B: Exclusive formula feeding
options.C: Family planning
options.D: Child labor prevention

explanation: Family planning is a foundational pillar that helps space births and protects women from high-risk pregnancies. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h2)

question: How does antenatal care directly contribute to saving a mother's life?

options.A: By preventing the mother from experiencing any labor pains
options.B: By identifying and treating potential complications before they become life-threatening
options.C: By guaranteeing that the baby will be born without any genetic disorders
options.D: By replacing the need for a skilled attendant during labor

explanation: Antenatal visits allow nurses and doctors to screen for conditions like high blood pressure and infections early, reducing emergency risks. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h2)

question: What does the first delay in the Three Delays Model refer to?

options.A: The time spent waiting for an ambulance on a bad road
options.B: The delay caused by nurses refusing to treat a patient
options.C: The time it takes for labor contractions to start
options.D: The delay in deciding to seek medical help

explanation: The first delay happens at the household or community level when family members fail to recognize danger signs or hesitate to seek care. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h3)

question: A pregnant woman in a remote village has severe bleeding, but her family wastes two hours trying traditional herbs before looking for transport. Which delay has occurred?

options.A: Delay in reaching care
options.B: Delay in deciding to seek care
options.C: Delay in post-delivery recovery
options.D: Delay in receiving care

explanation: Waiting to seek help because of trying home remedies or not understanding the urgency represents the first delay in the model. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h3)

question: What is the main purpose of using a partograph during intrapartum care?

options.A: To test the mother's blood sugar levels
options.B: To register the baby's name after birth
options.C: To calculate the total cost of hospital delivery
options.D: To monitor the progress of labor and detect problems early

explanation: The partograph is a visual tool used by nurses and midwives to track labor progress and maternal-fetal well-being. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h4)

question: Why is the immediate postpartum period considered the most critical time for postnatal care checks?

options.A: Because breast milk production stops if not checked immediately
options.B: Because most maternal deaths from bleeding happen shortly after delivery
options.C: Because the mother's blood pressure always drops to zero
options.D: Because the baby cries continuously during the first few hours

explanation: Postpartum hemorrhage is most likely to occur immediately after the placenta is delivered, making early observation essential. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h4)

question: Which service is provided in a Comprehensive EmONC (CEmONC) facility that is NOT part of a basic facility?

options.A: Basic neonatal resuscitation training
options.B: Provision of iron and folic acid supplements
options.C: Blood transfusions and caesarean sections
options.D: Administration of routine tetanus vaccines

explanation: Major surgeries like caesarean sections and blood banking are what upgrade a facility from basic to comprehensive EmONC. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h5)

question: A patient arrives at a primary health clinic with a severe postpartum hemorrhage that requires a blood transfusion. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Send the patient home with oral pain relievers
options.B: Stabilize the patient and quickly arrange transfer to a CEmONC facility
options.C: Perform a major surgical operation right there in the primary clinic
options.D: Wait for the bleeding to stop on its own before taking action

explanation: Basic clinics cannot handle blood transfusions or major surgery, so quick stabilization and emergency referral are mandatory. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h5)

question: What is a primary responsibility of a nurse-midwife during antenatal care visits?

options.A: Manufacturing iron and vitamin supplements
options.B: Performing major obstetric surgeries at primary clinics
options.C: Educating mothers on danger signs and proper nutrition
options.D: Building new roads for easy transport to hospitals

explanation: Nurse-midwives play a key role in health education, teaching women what to expect and when to seek urgent help. [learn more](GNS214_U1_T44#GNS214_U1_T44_h6)

question: Why is building a trusting relationship between the nurse and the pregnant woman so important?

options.A: It encourages the woman to report health problems and return for follow-up visits
options.B: It prevents the husband from being involved in family health decisions
options.C: It eliminates the need for any laboratory tests during pregnancy
